name: Afghanistan
funFacts: This country exports coal, grapes, tropical fruits, gum resins, and other nuts as its top five commodities — a list dominated by agricultural and botanical products with no petroleum or manufactured goods despite listing both natural gas and petroleum among its natural resources.

This country sends 42% of exports to Pakistan and 40% to India — over 80% flowing to just two immediate neighbors — one of the highest bilateral export concentrations among South and Central Asian nations.

This country's natural resources include precious and semiprecious stones alongside copper, chromite, talc, barites, lead, zinc, and coal — a mineral profile where gem-quality stones appear explicitly alongside industrial metals in one of the world's most mineralogically diverse landlocked nations.

This country's factbook notes two competing national holidays: the original Independence Day on 19 August (1919, independence from UK control of foreign affairs) and a 15 August holiday declared by the Taliban government in 2022 marking the anniversary of their return to power.

This country's industries include handwoven carpets as an explicitly named sector alongside cement, natural gas, and coal — one of the few nations where traditional textile craftsmanship is listed as a formal industrial category equal to extractive industries.

name: Angola
funFacts: This country's name derives from the title 'N'gola,' held by the kings of the Ndongo kingdom in the 15th century — a royal title that Portuguese explorers heard and adapted into the country's modern name.

This country gained independence on 11 November 1975 from Portugal — not from France or Britain as most neighboring African nations did — reflecting a Portuguese colonial heritage shared with only five other African nations.
This country's national symbol is the giant black sable antelope — a large bovine unique to its central highlands — one of the most distinctive national animal symbols chosen by any African nation.

This country sends 40% of its exports to China alone, with crude petroleum as its dominant export — a remarkably concentrated trade relationship that channels nearly half of all exports to a single buyer.

This country exports ships among its top five commodities alongside crude petroleum, diamonds, and natural gas — an unusual industrial export for an equatorial African nation reflecting its Atlantic port infrastructure.

name: Albania
funFacts: This country's local name — Shqiperia — derives from the Albanian word for 'eagle,' making it literally the 'Land of the Eagles,' and the black double-headed eagle remains its national symbol.
This country's official language descends specifically from the Tosk dialect of Albanian, distinguishing it linguistically from all its neighbors who speak Slavic or Greek languages.
This country exports garments and footwear as its top commodities, sending over 40% of its exports to Italy alone — a uniquely lopsided trade relationship among Balkan nations.
This country sits at the southeastern tip of the Adriatic coast, with its highest peak, Maja e Korabit at 2,764 m, forming the border with North Macedonia.
This country is the only nation in Europe that sheltered its entire Jewish population during World War II, a tradition rooted in the Albanian code of honor called Besa, meaning 'to keep the promise.'

name: Andorra
funFacts: This country is the last surviving remnant of the Frankish buffer states created by Charlemagne in 795 to stop the Moorish advance into Christian France, making it a living relic of medieval geopolitics.
This country is governed by two co-princes simultaneously — the French head of state and the Spanish Bishop of Urgell — a feudal arrangement that has persisted in modified form since 1278.
This country's lowest point is 840 m above sea level, making it the only European country whose lowest geographic point is higher than most of its neighbors' mountain towns.
This country attracts approximately 8 million visitors per year to a nation of fewer than 86,000 people, drawn primarily by skiing, duty-free shopping, and its mature low-tax banking sector.

This country uses the euro as its currency despite not being an EU member, and its top exports include paintings and orthopedic appliances — an unusual mix that reflects its wealthy, tourism-driven economy.

name: United Arab Emirates
funFacts: This country lists only petroleum and natural gas as natural resources — one of the sparsest resource profiles in the Gulf — yet achieves a GDP per capita of $68,600 by combining oil wealth with a globally significant gold and broadcasting equipment re-export trade.

This country exports gold as its third-largest commodity despite having no domestic gold mines — a gold that transits through its trade hub infrastructure, making it one of the world's most significant gold re-export centers.

This country exports broadcasting equipment as one of its top five commodities alongside petroleum and gold — electronics for media and communications that position it as a re-export hub for technology goods flowing between Asia, Africa, and Europe.

This country borders only two nations — Oman and Saudi Arabia — yet serves as a primary export destination for dozens of African, Asian, and South American nations, reflecting a trade hub role vastly disproportionate to its minimal land borders.

This country's name explicitly describes its federal structure — the term 'united' names the federation, and 'emirates' names the type of constituent monarchies — making it one of the few countries whose official name contains a complete description of its governmental form.

name: Argentina
funFacts: This country's highest peak, Cerro Aconcagua at 6,962 meters, is the tallest mountain in the entire Western Hemisphere and the highest point in all of South America.

This country's name derives from the Latin word for 'silver,' reflecting early Spanish explorers' belief that the Río de la Plata region held vast silver deposits — a hope that largely proved unfounded.
This country is one of the world's leading exporters of soybean meal and soybean oil, with Brazil, the USA, Chile, China, and India among its top five trading partners.

This country celebrates two founding moments: Revolution Day on 25 May 1810, when colonists ousted the colonial viceroy, and Independence Day on 9 July 1816 — a six-year gap between uprising and formal independence.
This country's national symbol, the Sun of May, depicts a sun with a human face and appears on its flag — linking modern national identity directly to the May Revolution of 1810.

name: Armenia
funFacts: This country's primary national symbol is Mount Ararat — a snow-capped volcanic peak that sits entirely within the territory of neighboring Turkey — making it unique among nations whose primary national symbol lies beyond its own borders.

This country's industries include brandy production and diamond processing alongside metal-cutting machine tools — one of the few Caucasian nations where a premium distilled spirit and precious stone processing appear as formal industrial sectors.

This country's independence declaration of 21 September 1991 is its primary date, yet its factbook also notes a Kingdom of Armenia established in 321 B.C. — giving it one of the longest documented histories of continuous statehood of any post-Soviet republic.

This country sends 37% of its exports to Russia and 25% to the UAE — a distribution reflecting both its historical Soviet ties and its role as a re-export and transit economy for goods flowing between East and West.

This country exports gold, diamonds, copper ore, broadcasting equipment, and jewelry — a top-five list where both rough diamonds and finished jewelry appear alongside electronic broadcasting goods and raw metals.

name: Antigua and Barbuda
funFacts: This country's highest point is named Mount Obama, rising to 402 m above sea level.
This country is a two-island nation whose name combines the Spanish words for 'ancient' and 'bearded' — the latter possibly referring to lichen-covered fig trees on one of its islands.
This country gained independence on 1 November 1981 and counts the fallow deer as its national symbol.
This country exports refined petroleum and ships as its top commodities, with Suriname and Poland as its leading trade partners.
In 2017, one of this country's two islands was almost entirely destroyed by Hurricane Irma, forcing its entire population to evacuate to the other island.

name: Australia
funFacts: This country has no land borders — an island continent with zero border countries — whose 25,760-kilometer coastline faces the Indian and Pacific Oceans, making it the only country that occupies an entire continent without sharing a land border with any other nation.

This country's natural resources include opals alongside diamonds, rare earth elements, lithium, and uranium — one of the most mineralogically diverse resource inventories of any nation in the factbook, spanning gemstones, strategic metals, nuclear materials, and conventional fossil fuels.

This country's national symbols include four distinct items: the Commonwealth Star (a seven-pointed Star of Federation), the golden wattle tree, the kangaroo, and the emu — one of the most extensive official national symbol sets of any country in the Southern Hemisphere.

This country's highest point, Mount Kosciuszko at only 2,228 meters, is the lowest national high point of any continental-sized nation on Earth — reflecting that this geologically ancient and stable landmass has been worn down over hundreds of millions of years of erosion.

This country sends 37% of its exports to China — its single largest commodity being iron ore — with Japan and South Korea receiving the next highest shares, making its top three export markets exclusively northeast Asian economies.

name: Austria
funFacts: This country's name means 'eastern realm' in German, a reference to its historic role as the easternmost extension of Bavarian and Germanic settlement, and it remains the only major German-speaking country whose name encodes that directional origin.

This country declared permanent neutrality by constitutional law in 1955 as the condition for ending Allied occupation after World War II, which is why it joined the EU in 1995 but has never joined NATO.
This country is landlocked and surrounded by eight neighbors — the most of any European country — including Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Germany, Czechia, Slovakia, Hungary, Slovenia, and Italy.

This country exports vaccines and packaged medicine alongside cars, with its lowest point being the Neusiedler See at 115 m — a shallow steppe lake shared with Hungary — and its highest the Grossglockner at 3,798 m.

This country was once the center of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, which at its peak controlled much of Central Europe; its capital Vienna served as one of the great imperial courts of the world until 1918.

name: Azerbaijan
funFacts: This country's name translates as 'Fire Keeper' or 'The Land of Fire,' derived from the word 'azer' meaning fire — a name that refers to the ancient natural gas seeps that once caused fires to burn spontaneously at the surface.
This country's national symbol is flames of fire — one of the only nations in the world to choose fire itself rather than an animal, plant, or celestial body as its primary national emblem.
This country's lowest point is the Caspian Sea at -28 meters — meaning parts of its territory sit below sea level along one of the world's largest enclosed bodies of water.
This country sends 37% of its exports to Italy and 19% to Turkey — with over half of all crude and refined petroleum flowing west toward European Mediterranean buyers.
This country exports electricity alongside crude petroleum and natural gas — one of the few Caspian oil-producing nations to list electrical power itself as a top-five export commodity.

name: Burundi
funFacts: This country has a GDP per capita of only $800 — among the lowest in the world — yet its natural resources include cobalt, niobium, tantalum, vanadium, and rare earth oxides: strategic minerals critical to modern electronics and aerospace.

This country has two capitals: Gitega serves as the political capital, while Bujumbura — the former capital on Lake Tanganyika's shore — functions as the commercial capital, splitting governance and commerce between two cities.

This country sends 59% of its exports to the UAE — primarily gold and coffee — making it one of the most UAE-dependent African economies, channeling the majority of its goods through a single Gulf state.

This country gained independence in 1962 from a UN trusteeship under Belgian administration — a different colonial pathway from most African nations, which were directly colonized by European powers rather than administered through a UN framework.

This country's lowest point, Lake Tanganyika at 772 meters above sea level, sits higher than the sea-level coastlines of coastal neighbors to the west — yet the lake itself plunges to extraordinary depth, forming one of Africa's most dramatic geographic contrasts.

name: Belgium
funFacts: This country is one of the few in the world with three official languages — Dutch, French, and German — and long-standing constitutional tensions between its Dutch-speaking Flemish north and French-speaking Walloon south have reshaped its government into a complex federal structure.
This country hosts the headquarters of both the EU and NATO in its capital Brussels, making it arguably the administrative center of Western collective security and economic integration.

This country has an urbanization rate of 98.2% — the highest in continental Europe — yet its highest point, Botrange, reaches only 694 m, making it one of the flattest and most densely settled nations on Earth.

This country derives its name from the Belgae, an ancient Celtic tribal confederation described by Julius Caesar as inhabiting the region between the English Channel and the Rhine in the first centuries B.C.

This country exports refined petroleum and natural gas as its top two commodities despite having almost no domestic fossil fuel resources, functioning as a major refining and transit hub for energy flowing to France, the Netherlands, and Germany.

name: Benin
funFacts: This country has two capitals: Porto-Novo serves as the constitutional capital, while Cotonou — the country's largest city — functions as the actual seat of government, splitting its governmental identity between two cities.

This country sends 42% of its exports to the UAE and 20% to Bangladesh — an unusually concentrated trade profile linking a small West African economy to Gulf and South Asian markets rather than European ones.

This country's name may derive from the Arabic word 'bani' meaning 'sons,' linked to the local Bini ethnic group — and the country was formerly known as Dahomey, after the powerful Fon kingdom of that name.

This country exports gold, cotton, and cashews as its top three commodities despite having only small offshore oil deposits — making agriculture and commodity trading more central to its economy than petroleum.

This country's highest point is an unnamed elevation of only 675 meters — one of the lowest national high points in Africa — reflecting its flat coastal and plateau geography along the Gulf of Guinea.

name: Burkina Faso
funFacts: This country's name translates as 'Land of the Worthy Men,' derived from Dyula words meaning 'worthy' (burkina) and 'land' or 'father village' (faso) — one of the most inspirational and morally explicit national names in Africa.

This country sends 72% of its exports to Switzerland — primarily gold — one of the most concentrated export relationships on the continent, where a landlocked Sahelian country directs nearly three-quarters of its goods to a single European nation.

This country's highest point, Tena Kourou at 749 meters, is among the lowest national high points in West Africa — reflecting the flat, semi-arid Sahel terrain that covers most of its landlocked geography.

This country borders six nations — Benin, Cote d'Ivoire, Ghana, Mali, Niger, and Togo — more land neighbors than any of those individual countries borders each other, placing it at the geographic center of West Africa.

This country is landlocked and exports gold, cotton, oil seeds, and cashews — an entirely agricultural and artisanal-mining export profile with no petroleum or industrial metals in its top five commodities.

name: Bangladesh
funFacts: This country's entire top-five export list consists of garments, footwear, fabric, textiles, and trunks — the only South Asian nation whose top exports are exclusively manufactured clothing and textile goods with no petroleum, metals, or unprocessed agricultural commodities.

This country gained independence on 16 December 1971 from Pakistan rather than directly from a colonial power — making it the only South Asian nation to have achieved independence from another formerly colonized country rather than from a European empire.

This country celebrates two distinct independence-related national holidays: Independence Day on 26 March (1971), when independence was declared, and Victory Day on 16 December (1971), when the Liberation War concluded — the only South Asian nation with two formally recognized independence milestones.

This country's highest point, Mowdok Taung at only 1,060 meters, is the lowest national high point of any South Asian mainland nation — a reflection of its predominantly low-lying delta geography formed by the Ganges and Brahmaputra river systems.

This country borders only Burma and India — two neighbors — despite being one of the most densely populated nations on Earth, with an area of just 148,460 square kilometers containing over 170 million people.

name: Bulgaria
funFacts: This country's name is derived from the Bulgar tribes, a Central Asian Turkic group who merged with local Slavic peoples in the 7th century A.D. to create the first Bulgarian state — one of Europe's oldest continuously named nations.
This country is the only EU member state with a Black Sea coastline, bordered by Romania to the north, Serbia and North Macedonia to the west, Greece and Turkey to the south.
This country exports refined petroleum and refined copper alongside garments and wheat, making it one of the few Balkan economies with significant metal-refining and energy-processing industries.
This country joined NATO in 2004, the EU in 2007, and then the Schengen Area for air and sea travel in 2024 — one of the last EU members to complete that final step of borderless travel integration.
This country has a Turkish-speaking Muslim minority comprising nearly 8% of the population, a legacy of over four centuries of Ottoman rule that ended only in 1878 when it gained autonomy.

name: Bahrain
funFacts: This country's name means 'the two seas' in Arabic — referring to the seawater bodies on each side of its island archipelago — one of the few nations in the world named after the seas that surround it rather than its own land.

This country's natural resources include pearls alongside oil and gas — a listing that reflects its ancient role as the Persian Gulf's primary pearl-diving hub, centuries before petroleum was discovered.

This country exports aluminum wire and refined aluminum alongside refined petroleum — a non-petroleum industrial export profile unusual among small Gulf states, reflecting a significant aluminum smelting industry.
This country's industries include Islamic and offshore banking — giving it a banking sector formally built around Islamic finance principles that distinguishes it from most of its Gulf neighbors.

This country's highest point, Jabal ad Dukhan at only 135 meters, is the lowest national high point in the entire Middle East — reflecting that this small island archipelago barely rises above sea level.

name: The Bahamas
funFacts: This country's highest point is an unnamed elevation of only 64 meters on Cat Island — one of the lowest national high points in the Caribbean — reflecting that its 700-island archipelago consists entirely of low-lying coral formations with no significant terrain.

This country exports ships as its second-largest commodity alongside refined petroleum and aluminum — maritime vessel re-registration and oil bunkering being significant industries for an archipelago positioned along major Atlantic shipping lanes.

This country's export partners include Zimbabwe at 16% and Côte d'Ivoire at 14% — two African nations accounting for nearly a third of its exports — an unusual African trade orientation for a Caribbean island nation driven by ship registration rather than traditional commodity trade.

This country's natural resources include aragonite — a specific crystalline form of calcium carbonate used in aquaculture and water treatment — listed alongside salt and timber, with aragonite appearing in virtually no other Caribbean nation's resource inventory.

This country's national symbols are the blue marlin, the flamingo, and the yellow elderflower — three distinct symbols spanning a large pelagic fish, a wading bird, and a flowering plant — one of the most diverse official national symbol sets in the Caribbean.

name: Bosnia and Herzegovina
funFacts: This country's very name encodes medieval history: the northern half is named for the Bosna River, while the southern half, Herzegovina, means 'dukedom' — derived from the Old Serbian word herceg, meaning 'duke.'
This country has a coastline of only 20 km on the Adriatic, one of the shortest of any coastal country in Europe, giving it just enough sea access for a single port town.

This country's 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement, signed in Dayton, Ohio, created a unique governmental structure with two largely autonomous entities — the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republika Srpska — that share a single internationally recognized state.

This country exports footwear and electricity as its top commodities, and sends its largest share of exports to Germany, Croatia, and Serbia — three of its closest neighbors that were also parties to the 1990s conflict.
This country has three official languages — Bosnian, Serbian, and Croatian — all mutually intelligible South Slavic tongues, spoken by its three main constituent peoples: Bosniaks, Serbs, and Croats.

name: Belarus
funFacts: This country's name literally means 'White Rus' in Slavic, combining the word for 'white' with the ancient East Slavic ethnic name — a linguistic echo preserved in both its official name and everyday language.
This country is the only European nation whose southern territory was contaminated by fallout from the 1986 Chornobyl nuclear accident, which occurred across the border in northern Ukraine.
This country is landlocked and shares borders with Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Russia, and Ukraine, and its highest point is just 346 m — one of the flattest countries on the continent.

This country exports fertilizers and rapeseed oil as top commodities, with 34% of its exports going to China — a trade profile that reflects its close alignment with non-Western partners after Western sanctions.

This country is the only European nation that has retained closer political and economic ties to Russia than any other former Soviet republic, formalizing a two-state union treaty with Russia in 1999.

name: Belize
funFacts: This country is the only Central American nation where English is the official language, and its capital was moved inland to Belmopan after a devastating hurricane hit the former coastal capital.
This country's highest point is Doyle's Delight at 1,124 m, and it borders both Guatemala and Mexico — the only country in Central America that borders Mexico.
This country exports raw sugar, bananas, fish, shellfish, and refined petroleum, with the USA and UK as its top two trade partners.
This country's name may derive from the Spanish pronunciation of Scottish explorer Peter Wallace's surname, or from the Maya word 'belix' meaning 'muddy-watered,' referring to the Belize River.
This country's national symbols include Baird's tapir, the keel-billed toucan, and the black orchid, reflecting its rich biodiversity and forest heritage.

name: Bolivia
funFacts: This country is one of only two landlocked nations in South America, with no access to the sea — its lowest point, the Rio Paraguay, sits at 90 meters above sea level, well above the ocean.

This country holds the unusual distinction of having two capital cities: La Paz serves as the administrative and executive capital, while Sucre functions as the constitutional, legislative, and judicial capital.

This country is named in honor of Simón Bolívar, a 19th-century independence leader — making it one of the few nations in the world named after a historical individual rather than a geographic or ethnic feature.

This country's natural resources include lithium, tin, tungsten, and antimony alongside silver and gold — a combination of rare and strategic metals found together in few other South American nations.

This country's national symbols include two distinct official flowers — the cantuta and the patuju — alongside the llama and the Andean condor, giving it one of the most elaborate sets of national symbols in the region.

name: Brazil
funFacts: This country's name derives from the brazil tree, a timber prized for its vivid red dye that once grew abundantly along its coast — making it one of the rare nations in the world named after a plant.
This country's Atlantic coastline stretches 7,491 kilometers — the longest in South America — and it shares land borders with every other South American nation except Chile and Ecuador.
This country sends 30% of its total exports to China alone — a higher share than any other large South American nation — with soybeans, crude petroleum, and iron ore as its top three commodities.

This country's natural resources include niobium, a rare metal used in high-strength steel alloys, listed alongside bauxite, gold, and platinum — one of the most diverse mineral endowments in the Western Hemisphere.
This country's national symbol is the Southern Cross constellation, one of the very few nations in the world to use a celestial grouping of stars as its primary national emblem.

name: Barbados
funFacts: This country's national symbols include Neptune's trident, a pelican, and the red bird of paradise flower known locally as the 'Pride of Barbados.'
This country became a republic in 2021, electing former Governor-General Sandra Mason as its first president — making it the most recently declared republic in the Caribbean.
This country's top export is liquor, followed by refined petroleum, packaged medicine, margarine, and baked goods.
This country has a coastline of just 97 km and a highest point of Mount Hillaby at 336 m, making it one of the flattest islands in the Caribbean.
This country's name is the plural of a Spanish word meaning 'the bearded ones,' which may refer to the beard-like leaves of the island's fig trees or to the beards of Carib inhabitants.

name: Brunei
funFacts: This country's GDP per capita of $79,200 is among the highest in Southeast Asia — generated almost entirely from petroleum and natural gas extraction on a small territory of only 5,765 square kilometers that is otherwise entirely encircled by Malaysian states on the island of Borneo.

This country borders only Malaysia — the only Southeast Asian nation with a single land neighbor — its territory forming two non-contiguous enclaves completely surrounded by Malaysian land and coastal waters.

This country's entire top-five export list consists of refined petroleum, natural gas, crude petroleum, hydrocarbons, and fertilizers — every top-five export being a hydrocarbon product or direct derivative, with no manufactured goods or agricultural commodities.

This country's national symbol is the royal parasol — a ceremonial object signifying sovereignty rather than an animal, plant, or celestial body — one of the most distinctively regal national symbols in all of Southeast Asia.

This country gained independence on 1 January 1984 from the United Kingdom — one of the last Southeast Asian nations to achieve sovereignty — its sultanate having been a British protectorate for nearly a century before independence.

name: Bhutan
funFacts: This country sends 92% of its exports to India — the highest export concentration to a single neighboring country among all South Asian nations — reflecting near-total economic integration with the one country that surrounds it on three sides.

This country's national symbol is the mythical thunder dragon, the druk — a creature from which the country's name in its own language derives — making its national emblem a creature from mythology rather than a living animal, plant, or celestial body.

This country exports aircraft alongside iron alloys, dolomite, semi-finished iron, and cement — a top-five list where aerospace hardware appears alongside industrial minerals, an unusual pairing for a landlocked Himalayan nation with no domestic aircraft manufacturing.

This country's natural resources are listed as only timber, hydropower, gypsum, and calcium carbonate — one of the sparsest resource profiles in South Asia — yet calcium carbonate production directly feeds its cement industry, one of its primary industrial sectors.

This country borders only China and India — the two most populous nations on Earth — yet has maintained its independence since 1907 through a formally recognized Treaty of Friendship with India that explicitly preserves Bhutanese sovereignty.

name: Botswana
funFacts: This country's name translates as 'Land of the Tswana,' referring to its largest ethnic group — one of a handful of African nations whose name directly describes its primary people in their own language.

This country's national symbol is the zebra — a uniquely striped animal associated with its vast wildlife reserves — while its GDP per capita of $18,100 makes it one of the wealthiest nations in sub-Saharan Africa.

This country exports diamonds, copper ore, insulated wire, and carbonates — with insulated wire and carbonates as unusual industrial commodities in a top-five export list otherwise dominated by raw minerals.
This country shares a border with Zambia of only 150 meters — one of the world's shortest bilateral land borders — at a point where four countries (Botswana, Namibia, Zambia, and Zimbabwe) converge.

This country's entire territory sits above 513 meters — even its lowest point, the junction of the Limpopo and Shashe Rivers, stands 513 meters above sea level — making it one of Africa's highest-elevation landlocked nations.

name: Central African Republic
funFacts: This country's name — 'Central African Republic' — is a self-descriptive geographic designation specifying its location on the continent, one of the most literally named countries in the world.

This country sends 54% of its exports to the UAE — primarily gold, wood, and diamonds — making it one of the most UAE-dependent African economies despite no historical or geographic connection to the Gulf.
This country's borders touch five nations — Cameroon, Chad, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, South Sudan, and Sudan — placing it at the crossroads where West, Central, and East Africa meet.
This country exports vehicle parts among its top five commodities alongside gold, diamonds, and timber — an unusual industrial export for a landlocked nation with a GDP per capita of only $1,100.

This country's lowest point, the Oubangui River at 335 meters above sea level, means its entire territory sits well above sea level despite being surrounded by flat Central African lowlands drained by the Congo River basin.

name: Canada
funFacts: This country has the world's longest coastline at 202,080 km — more than ten times that of its southern neighbor — yet shares land borders with only two other countries.
This country exports crude petroleum, cars, gold, natural gas, and refined petroleum as its top commodities, and its national symbols are the maple leaf and the beaver.
This country achieved union in 1867 but only fully formalized its constitutional independence from Britain in 1982, all while retaining ties to the British crown.
This country has two official languages — English and French — and its name likely derives from a Huron or Iroquois word meaning 'village or camp.'
This country is slightly larger than its southern neighbor by total area yet has a population of only about 39 million people, with its capital located in Ottawa.

name: Switzerland
funFacts: This country has four official national languages — German, French, Italian, and Romansh — and its national anthem exists in four corresponding versions; no other country in Europe has this many official languages with parity of status.

This country exports more gold by value than almost any other commodity — gold is its single largest export — reflecting its role as a global center for gold refining, trading, and vaulting, processing an estimated 70% of the world's gold supply.

This country did not officially become a member of the United Nations until 2002 — one of the last countries in the world to join — preserving a strict neutrality policy it has maintained since major European powers recognized its sovereignty in 1815.

This country's official name is the Swiss Confederation, with the Latin abbreviation CH (Confoederatio Helvetica) used on its currency and internet domain, derived from the Helvetii, the Celtic tribe that inhabited the region in Roman times.

This country is landlocked by five neighbors — Austria, France, Germany, Italy, and Liechtenstein — and its lowest point, Lake Maggiore at 195 m, is shared with Italy in the south, while its highest peak, Dufourspitze on Monte Rosa at 4,634 m, is the highest point in all of Switzerland.

name: Chile
funFacts: This country's highest peak, Nevado Ojos del Salado at 6,893 meters, is identified in its factbook data as the highest volcano in the world — a geological superlative that sets it apart from every neighbor.
This country's export economy is dominated by copper ore and refined copper, with China alone receiving 39% of its exports — one of the most copper-concentrated trade profiles of any nation on Earth.

This country's legislature meets in Valparaíso while its executive government is based in Santiago — an unusual split between two distinct governmental cities rather than one unified national capital.
This country's national symbols are the huemul, a rare mountain deer endemic to the Andes, and the Andean condor — both animals found almost exclusively within high-altitude Andean terrain.
This country's 6,435-kilometer Pacific coastline is the longest western coast of any South American nation, while its land territory is bounded by just three neighbors: Argentina, Bolivia, and Peru.

name: China
funFacts: This country's natural resources list names over 30 distinct minerals — from conventional coal, iron ore, and petroleum to rare industrial metals including gallium, germanium, hafnium, indium, and tantalum — one of the most extensive mineral resource inventories of any nation in the entire factbook dataset.

This country's hydropower potential is noted as the world's largest directly in its natural resources listing — an energy superlative embedded parenthetically within a resource list, reflecting its position as the world's leading generator of hydroelectric power.

This country borders 14 nations — more land neighbors than any other country on Earth — spanning from Russia and Mongolia in the north to Vietnam and Laos in the south and from Kazakhstan in the west to North Korea in the east.

This country's factbook describes it as the 'world leader in gross value of industrial output' — a direct global superlative embedded in its industries section — citing a complete range of production from coal mining to high-performance aircraft and space vehicles.

This country's national symbols are the dragon and the giant panda — combining a mythological creature central to its cultural identity with a real endangered animal found almost exclusively within its borders — a pairing unique among the world's major powers.

name: Cote d'Ivoire
funFacts: This country's name translates as 'Ivory Coast' in French, reflecting the ivory trade that drew European merchants to the region from the 15th to 17th centuries — and the government has long insisted this French name be used internationally.

This country has two capitals: Yamoussoukro functions as the legislative capital while Abidjan serves as the administrative and economic capital — splitting political and commercial functions between cities 240 km apart.

This country lists cocoa beans and palm oil directly among its natural resources alongside petroleum, diamonds, and manganese — one of the few African nations to formally classify agricultural commodities as primary natural resources.

This country exports cocoa beans as its second-largest commodity after gold, with cashews also in the top five — placing it among the world's top cocoa producers while exporting precious metals and tree nuts in the same shipments.

This country borders five West African nations — Burkina Faso, Ghana, Guinea, Liberia, and Mali — yet its top trading partners are Switzerland, the Netherlands, the USA, and Malaysia, reflecting a trade geography oriented far outside its immediate region.

name: Cameroon
funFacts: This country's name derives from the Portuguese phrase 'Rio dos Camaroes,' meaning 'River of Prawns,' given by 16th-century explorers who found abundant shrimp in the Wouri River estuary — making it one of the few nations named after a crustacean.
This country's highest point, Fako on Mont Cameroun at 4,045 meters, is an active volcano — one of the highest and most active volcanic peaks in West and Central Africa.

This country borders six nations — Central African Republic, Chad, Republic of the Congo, Equatorial Guinea, Gabon, and Nigeria — a level of multiple bordering that reflects its position at the geographic hinge of West and Central Africa.

This country exports crude petroleum, natural gas, gold, cocoa beans, and timber — a combination spanning hydrocarbons, precious metals, and tropical agricultural products found together in few other Central African nations.

This country's industries include aluminum production alongside petroleum refining and ship repair — one of the only Central African nations with a significant aluminum smelting sector alongside traditional resource extraction.

name: Congo DR
funFacts: This country has only 37 kilometers of Atlantic coastline — the shortest ocean access of any coastal country in Africa — a narrow strip at the mouth of the Congo River that is all that remains after colonial borders were drawn.

This country sends 69% of its exports to China — one of the highest single-country trade concentrations of any large African nation — with cobalt and refined copper as the dominant commodities powering global battery and electronics industries.

This country's natural resources include cobalt, niobium, tantalum, and coltan — rare minerals essential for smartphones, electric vehicles, and aerospace alloys — giving it enormous strategic importance in global technology supply chains.

This country's population of over 119 million and area of 2,344,858 square kilometers make it the largest and most populous nation in Central Africa — yet its GDP per capita is only $1,500 despite possessing enormous mineral wealth.

This country's highest point, Pic Marguerite on Mont Ngaliema (also called Mount Stanley) at 5,110 meters, rises from the Rwenzori Mountains in the far east — a glaciated massif that towers over an otherwise low-lying tropical basin.

name: Congo
funFacts: This country's capital, Brazzaville, sits directly across the Congo River from Kinshasa — the capital of a different country, the Democratic Republic of the Congo — making these two capitals one of the closest pairs of distinct national capitals anywhere in the world.
This country sends 46% of its exports to China and 23% to the UAE — nearly 70% going to just two buyers — making it among the most export-concentrated economies in Central Africa.

This country was formerly known as the People's Republic of the Congo between 1969 and 1992 — a Marxist-Leninist single-party state that later transitioned to multiparty democracy, giving it a distinct political trajectory from its neighbors.

This country exports refined copper as its second-largest commodity alongside crude petroleum, gold, and timber — a combination spanning raw hydrocarbons, refined metals, and forest products within a single top-five list.

This country's highest point, Mont Nabeba at only 1,020 meters, is among the lowest national high points in Central Africa — reflecting its position in the equatorial Congo basin, a vast lowland that spans much of this region.

name: Colombia
funFacts: This country is the only nation in South America with coastlines on both the Caribbean Sea (1,760 km) and the Pacific Ocean (1,448 km) — giving it dual maritime access shared by no other South American state.

This country is named directly after the explorer Christopher Columbus — and its highest peak, Pico Cristóbal Colón at 5,730 meters, also carries Columbus's name, creating a unique double tribute to the same historical figure.
This country's natural resources include emeralds alongside petroleum, coal, gold, and nickel — a gemstone listed as a key mineral resource in a way found in no other South American nation's data.

This country's top export is crude petroleum, yet it also lists coffee among its top five exports alongside coal and gold — a rare combination of hydrocarbons, precious metals, and premium agricultural commodity.
This country emerged from the dissolution of Gran Colombia in 1830 — the same event that created Ecuador and Venezuela — making all three nations direct successors of a single short-lived federation.

name: Comoros
funFacts: This country's name derives from the Arabic phrase 'al qamar,' meaning 'the moon' — a celestial name that distinguishes it from every other African nation and reflects centuries of Arab maritime influence on the archipelago.

This country's exports include cloves, essential oils, and vanilla alongside ships and scrap iron — one of the few nations in the world where aromatic spices and fragrant plant oils appear alongside industrial commodities in the top-five export list.

This country's listed natural resources consist only of fish — one of the sparsest resource profiles of any African nation — yet it sustains an economy through fishing, tourism, and the distillation of aromatic plant oils.

This country's industries include perfume distillation — one of the only nations in the world to list the extraction of aromatic plant essences as a formal sector — reflecting its position as a global supplier of fragrant plant oils.

This country exports cloves and essential oils primarily to Indonesia (25%) and India (23%) — sending its spice exports eastward to Asia rather than northward to Europe, reflecting centuries-old Indian Ocean trade routes.

name: Cape Verde
funFacts: This country was entirely uninhabited when Portuguese explorers discovered and colonized it in the 15th century — one of the few modern nations with no indigenous pre-colonial population.

This country's name derives from the Cape Verde peninsula on the Senegalese coast — the westernmost point of Africa and the nearest mainland to the islands — even though the islands themselves are not on that cape.
This country's highest point, Mt. Fogo at 2,829 meters, is an active volcano on Fogo Island — one of the most dramatically elevated volcanic islands off the West African coast.

This country sends 46% of its exports to Spain and 9% to Portugal — the Iberian Peninsula nations that colonized and subsequently governed it — reflecting a trade relationship shaped by centuries of colonial ties.

This country exports fish, refined petroleum, railway cargo containers, and shellfish — an unusual mix where seafood and industrial transport containers appear together in the top-five export list of a small Atlantic archipelago.

name: Costa Rica
funFacts: This country's name means 'rich coast' in Spanish, a name given by Christopher Columbus in 1502 in reference to the region's abundant vegetation and water.
This country's top exports are medical instruments and integrated circuits — not tropical crops — making it unusual among its Central American neighbors.
This country has no military, a distinction stemming from its 1948 civil war, and its highest point is Cerro Chirripo at 3,819 m.
This country's national bird is the yiguirro, also known as the clay-colored thrush, and its capital is San José.

This country gained independence from Spain on 15 September 1821, the same date shared by Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, and Nicaragua, but unlike them, it has had only two brief periods of political violence in its history.

name: Cuba
funFacts: This country is the largest island in the Caribbean by area at 110,860 sq km, with a coastline of 3,735 km and a highest point of Pico Turquino at 1,974 m.
This country's top exports are tobacco, nickel, and liquor, and its leading trade partner is China, which receives 34% of its exports.
This country's national holiday is the 'Triumph of the Revolution' on 1 January, and its national symbol is the royal palm.
This country formally became an independent republic on 20 May 1902 after its independence from Spain was recognized on 10 December 1898, following US intervention in the Spanish-American War.
This country contains significant deposits of cobalt and nickel, and its industries include pharmaceuticals, tobacco processing, and sugar — alongside petroleum and cobalt mining.

name: Cyprus
funFacts: This country's very name is the ancient source of the word 'copper' — derived from the Sumerian kabar and Greek Kupros — because the island's copper mines were so productive in antiquity that the metal was named after it.

This country is an island in the eastern Mediterranean with no land borders, yet it is an EU member — though EU law is suspended in the northern portion controlled by Turkey since 1974 and recognized only by Ankara.

This country exports ships as its single largest commodity, along with refined petroleum and packaged medicine, with its top export partners including Libya, Lebanon, and Bermuda — an unusually Mediterranean and offshore-finance-oriented trade profile.

This country's capital, Nicosia (Lefkosia/Lefkosa), is the last divided capital city in Europe, split between the internationally recognized Republic of Cyprus and the Turkish-controlled north by a UN buffer zone.

This country's national symbol is the Cypriot mouflon, a rare wild sheep endemic to the island, alongside the white dove — two symbols that together evoke both the island's unique wildlife and aspirations for peace.

name: Czech Republic
funFacts: This country underwent what historians call the 'Velvet Divorce' on 1 January 1993, peacefully splitting from Slovakia without a single shot fired, after first having experienced the 'Velvet Revolution' that ended communist rule in 1989.

This country formally added the short-form name 'Czechia' in 2016 while retaining its full official name, Czech Republic — a rare modern example of a country officially adopting a new short-form name for international use.

This country is landlocked and entirely surrounded by four neighbors — Germany, Austria, Slovakia, and Poland — yet its highest peak, Snezka at 1,602 m, is modest compared to the Alpine countries on its borders.
This country exports cars and vehicle parts as its top commodities, sending nearly 29% of its exports to Germany alone — the most Germany-dependent trade relationship of any EU economy.

This country produces the most beer per capita of any country in the world, a reputation rooted in centuries of Bohemian brewing tradition that gave the world the Pilsner style, originally developed in Plzen (Pilsen).

name: Germany
funFacts: This country is Europe's largest economy and its most populous nation after Russia, yet it was divided into two separate states — West Germany and East Germany — for 45 years before reunification on 3 October 1990.

This country's lowest point, Neuendorf bei Wilster at -3.5 m, lies in the flat northern lowlands near the North Sea, while its highest point, the Zugspitze at 2,963 m, rises in the Bavarian Alps — a country that spans from reclaimed coastal marshland to high alpine terrain.

This country exports more cars and vehicle parts than any other European nation, with the USA, France, the Netherlands, China, and Italy as its five largest partners — an export profile dominated by automotive engineering.
This country recognizes four official minority languages — Danish, Frisian, Sorbian, and Romani — alongside German, acknowledging linguistic communities whose roots predate the German state itself.

This country's National Day commemorates not independence or revolution but reunification — 3 October 1990 — making it unique among major European nations in celebrating the healing of a Cold War division as its founding civic moment.

name: Djibouti
funFacts: This country's lowest point, Lac Assal at -155 meters below sea level, is the deepest depression in Africa — a volcanic salt lake that sits lower than any other point on the continent.

This country sends 77% of its exports to Ethiopia — its landlocked neighbor — serving as Ethiopia's primary port of access to the sea, making this tiny coastal nation's economy deeply intertwined with its far larger neighbor.

This country's export commodities include raw sugar, seed oils, cars, palm oil, and rice — none of which are produced domestically in significant quantities, reflecting an economy built primarily on re-export trade through its strategic port.

This country's name and its capital share the exact same name — Djibouti — making it one of the few countries in the world where nation and capital are completely identical rather than merely similar.

This country borders only three nations — Eritrea, Ethiopia, and Somalia — yet its position at the southern approach to the Red Sea gives it strategic maritime importance vastly disproportionate to its land area of 23,200 square kilometers.

name: Dominica
funFacts: This country was named by Christopher Columbus for the day of the week he spotted it — Sunday, 3 November 1493 — making it one of the few nations named after a day of the week.
This country was the last of the Caribbean islands to be colonized by Europeans, due chiefly to fierce resistance from the native Carib people, and it gained independence on 3 November 1978.
This country's highest point is Morne Diablotins at 1,447 m, the tallest peak in the Eastern Caribbean, giving it a mountainous, volcanic interior unlike most neighboring islands.
This country's national symbols are the sisserou parrot and the Carib wood flower; the sisserou parrot is endemic to this island and appears on its flag.
This country's capital is Roseau, and in 1980 it became the first Caribbean nation to elect a female prime minister when Mary Eugenia Charles came to power.

name: Denmark
funFacts: This country shares a land border with Canada — a 1.3 km boundary on Hans Island between Greenland and Ellesmere Island — making it the only European country with a land border on the North American continent.

This country's highest point, Store Mollehoj, reaches only 171 m, making it one of the flattest countries in Europe, yet its coastline stretches 7,314 km — longer than most mountainous European nations — thanks to its deeply indented peninsulas and hundreds of islands.
This country is the world's leading manufacturer of wind turbines and a global leader in pharmaceuticals and medical equipment, exporting packaged medicine and vaccines as its top commodities.

This country is the only Scandinavian nation to have joined NATO at its founding in 1949 and also the first Nordic EU member, joining the EEC in 1973, though it has maintained opt-outs from the euro, EU defense, and justice policies.
This country's lowest point is the Lammefjord at -7 m, a former fjord drained for farmland in the 19th century — one of the most dramatic land-reclamation projects in Nordic history.

name: Dominican Republic
funFacts: This country declared independence on 27 February 1844 — not from a European colonial power, but from Haiti, which had ruled the eastern two-thirds of Hispaniola for 22 years.
This country shares the island of Hispaniola with Haiti and contains both the highest point in the Caribbean, Pico Duarte at 3,098 m, and the lowest point, Lago Enriquillo at -46 m.
This country's top exports are medical instruments, tobacco, and gold, and the USA receives 52% of its exports — the highest share of any country in this region.
This country's name derives from 'Santo Domingo,' meaning 'holy Sunday' in Spanish, after explorers settled there on a Sunday in 1496.
This country's national bird is the palmchat, a species found only on the island of Hispaniola, making it a uniquely identifying national symbol.

name: Algeria
funFacts: This country's natural resources are listed as only petroleum, natural gas, and gypsum — one of the sparsest mineral profiles for such a large nation — reflecting that most of its territory is covered by the Sahara Desert.

This country's national holiday includes both Independence Day (5 July 1962) and Revolution Day (1 November 1954) — commemorating not just liberation but the specific guerrilla uprising that launched the independence war.

This country exports iron bars as one of its top five commodities alongside natural gas, crude petroleum, and fertilizers — an unusual industrial product for an oil-exporting African nation reflecting its steel industry.

This country's national symbols include the fennec fox — the world's smallest wild dog species, adapted to desert life — alongside the star and crescent, making it one of few nations to use a diminutive desert mammal as a national emblem.

This country's lowest point, Chott Melrhir at -40 meters, is a salt lake below sea level — a geographic anomaly in a country whose vast territory is otherwise occupied by Saharan plateau rising far above sea level.

name: Ecuador
funFacts: This country's name is the Spanish word for 'equator,' as the geographic equator passes directly through its territory — making it one of the few countries in the world named after a line of latitude.

This country's top two export markets are the USA (22%) and China (21%) — an almost perfectly balanced split between the world's two largest economies, a trade profile unlike any other South American nation.

This country's exports include crude petroleum, shellfish, bananas, fish, and gold — an unusually diverse mix of hydrocarbons, seafood, tropical fruit, and precious metals within a single top-five list.

This country celebrates its National Day on 10 August — the independence of Quito in 1809 — though full independence from Spain wasn't completed until 24 May 1822, a thirteen-year gap between uprising and sovereignty.

This country shares land borders with only two neighbors — Colombia to the north and Peru to the south — yet maintains a 2,237-km Pacific coastline that gives it direct maritime access to global markets.

name: Egypt
funFacts: This country's national holiday celebrates Revolution Day — the 23 July 1952 military coup that ended the monarchy — rather than an independence date, reflecting that this ancient civilization traces continuity through millennia rather than a single founding moment.

This country's name derives from the ancient Greek 'Aguptos,' itself derived from the Egyptian phrase for its ancient capital Memphis — making its modern name a layered transformation from a 3,000-year-old place name.

This country's lowest point, the Qattara Depression at -133 meters, is a vast natural basin in the Sahara whose floor lies well below sea level — a geographic anomaly covering an area larger than many small nations.

This country exports refined petroleum, natural gas, fertilizers, and garments as its top four commodities — a combination of hydrocarbons, chemicals, and textile manufacturing that makes it one of Africa's most industrially diverse exporters.

This country's national symbols include the golden eagle and the white lotus — a pairing that directly echoes ancient Egyptian iconography, linking the modern republic's national identity to one of the world's oldest recorded civilizations.

name: Eritrea
funFacts: This country's name derives from the ancient Greek 'Erythra Thalassa,' meaning 'Red Sea' — named directly after the body of water forming its eastern border, making it one of the few countries named after an adjacent sea.

This country gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993, following a 30-year independence war — one of the only African nations whose post-colonial sovereignty came from another African country rather than a European power.

This country's 2,234 kilometers of coastline span both its Red Sea mainland (1,151 km) and its Red Sea islands (1,083 km) — with nearly half of its entire coastline consisting of island shorelines scattered across the southern Red Sea.

This country sends 67% of its exports to China and 26% to the UAE — with copper ore and zinc ore as its dominant commodities — making it one of the most export-concentrated African economies relative to just two trading partners.
This country's national symbol is the camel — a desert-adapted animal that reflects the country's Red Sea coastal desert environment and the pastoral heritage of its diverse ethnic communities.

name: Spain
funFacts: This country's highest point is not on the Iberian Peninsula but on the Canary Islands — Pico de Teide on Tenerife at 3,718 m — an active volcano that is the third-tallest volcanic structure in the world from its ocean base.
This country is the only nation in Europe that shares a land border with an African country: Morocco, via the Spanish cities of Ceuta and Melilla, which are enclaves on the North African coast.

This country has four co-official regional languages in addition to Castilian Spanish — Catalan, Galician, Basque, and Aranese — with Basque being the only language in Western Europe with no known linguistic relatives.

This country endured a devastating civil war from 1936 to 1939 followed by nearly four decades of dictatorship under Francisco Franco, transitioning to parliamentary democracy only after his death in 1975.

This country is the eurozone's fourth-largest economy and exports cars, packaged medicine, vehicle parts, and refined petroleum as its top commodities, with France and Germany together absorbing 25% of its exports.

name: Estonia
funFacts: This country's name derives from the Baltic word aueist, meaning 'waterside dwellers,' and it has a coastline of 3,794 km — remarkably long for a small nation — due to its deeply indented Baltic shore and thousands of small islands.

This country is one of the world's most digitally advanced societies, having pioneered e-governance, digital voting, and e-residency, and was the first former Soviet republic to adopt the euro, in 2011.

This country's natural resources include oil shale, which powers its electricity sector, making it unusual among EU members for generating significant electricity from domestic shale rather than imported fossil fuels.
This country exports prefabricated buildings as one of its top five commodities alongside cars and broadcasting equipment — a distinctive export that reflects its advanced wood-construction industry.

This country has the barn swallow as its national bird and the cornflower as its national flower — both symbols tied to its agricultural and rural identity that distinguish it from its Baltic neighbors Latvia and Lithuania.

name: Ethiopia
funFacts: This country is described as one of the oldest independent nations on Earth, with sovereignty traceable to the Aksumite Kingdom at least 2,000 years ago — a mainland African nation never colonized by a European power.

This country's top export is coffee, followed by garments, dried legumes, cut flowers, and oil seeds — with coffee as the single most valuable export in an otherwise agriculture-dominated trade profile.

This country exports cut flowers among its top five commodities alongside coffee — one of Africa's significant flower exporters, requiring sophisticated cold-chain logistics for a landlocked nation to deliver perishable blooms to foreign markets.

This country's lowest point, the Danakil Depression at -125 meters below sea level, sits in a volcanic rift zone — a dramatic contrast to the country's high central plateau, reflecting one of the most extreme elevation gradients of any African nation.

This country borders six nations — Djibouti, Eritrea, Kenya, Somalia, South Sudan, and Sudan — making it the African nation with the most neighboring countries among those entirely landlocked, reflecting its central position in the Horn of Africa.

name: Finland
funFacts: This country was the only Nordic state to join the euro at its launch in January 1999, while its Scandinavian neighbors Sweden, Norway, and Denmark retained their own currencies.

This country spent over a century as a grand duchy of Russia before declaring independence in 1917, and successfully defended that independence in World War II by cooperating with Germany against Soviet invasion — the only democratic nation to do so.

This country's local name, Suomi, may derive from suo ('marsh') and maa ('land') — 'land of marshes' — reflecting a landscape dominated by over 180,000 lakes and extensive wetlands, giving it among the highest lake-to-land ratios in the world.

This country exports paper, steel, wood pulp, and ships as its top commodities, with the USA and Germany tied as its largest export partners — an export profile that reflects its dual identity as a Nordic forest economy and advanced industrial nation.

This country joined NATO in April 2023 following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, becoming the 31st member and ending decades of military non-alignment — one of the most significant strategic shifts in post-Cold War European security.

name: Fiji
funFacts: This country exports water as its top commodity — one of the very few nations in the world whose single largest export by value is bottled water — a natural product bottled from its island springs and sold primarily to the United States, which receives 32% of its total exports.

This country's national symbol is the Fijian canoe — a traditional ocean-going vessel rather than an animal, plant, or celestial body — one of the few Pacific Island nations whose primary national emblem is a watercraft reflecting its seafaring heritage.

This country's exports include raw sugar alongside water and fish — a plantation agricultural commodity appearing in a top-five list that also includes bottled water and garments — reflecting a diversified small-island economy spanning agriculture, natural springs, and textile manufacturing.

This country's natural resources include offshore oil potential alongside timber, fish, gold, copper, and hydropower — the only Pacific Island nation in the region to list potential offshore petroleum as a named resource, though not yet in commercial production.

This country exports garments as a top-five commodity alongside water, fish, and sugar — one of the few Pacific Island nations to include manufactured textile goods in its top exports — reflecting an export-processing textile industry operating alongside its agricultural and fisheries sectors.

name: France
funFacts: This country is the world's leading exporter of aircraft and the only European country with overseas territories that are constitutionally part of the nation itself — including French Guiana in South America, Martinique and Guadeloupe in the Caribbean, Mayotte off Africa, and Réunion in the Indian Ocean.
This country's highest point, Mont Blanc at 4,810 m, is the tallest peak in the Alps and in all of Western Europe, while its lowest point, the Rhone River delta, sits at -2 m below sea level.

This country shares borders with eight neighbors — Andorra, Belgium, Germany, Italy, Luxembourg, Monaco, Spain, and Switzerland — the most of any country in Western Europe, reflecting its central position on the continent.

This country exports aircraft and gas turbines alongside cars and packaged medicine, making it Europe's pre-eminent aerospace power and one of only two European nations (with the UK) that are permanent members of the UN Security Council.

This country established the metric system, the Napoleonic Code of law, and the Declaration of the Rights of Man — foundational contributions to modern governance and measurement that shaped legal and scientific systems worldwide.

name: Micronesia
funFacts: This country's coastline of 6,112 kilometers is vastly disproportionate to its land area of only 702 square kilometers — giving it one of the highest coastline-to-land-area ratios of any sovereign nation in the world, reflecting hundreds of islands spread across a vast stretch of the western Pacific.

This country exports diamonds as a top-three commodity alongside fish and garments — an island nation in the Pacific with no diamond resources listed — whose diamond export reflects re-export or transit trade rather than any domestic mining activity.
This country sends 64% of its exports to Thailand — the highest concentration to a single buyer among Micronesian nations — primarily fish, with the remainder going to China and the Philippines.

This country's national symbols include four five-pointed white stars on a light blue field and the hibiscus flower — the four stars representing the four island groups that make up its territory — combined with a tropical flower as a natural emblem.

This country gained independence on 3 November 1986 from a US-administered UN trusteeship — the same year as the Marshall Islands — both Pacific Island nations achieving sovereignty simultaneously after decades of US strategic administration following World War II.

name: Gabon
funFacts: This country's name derives from the Portuguese word 'gabão,' meaning 'cloak,' used by early explorers to describe the shape of the Komo River estuary — making it one of the few nations named after a garment.
This country's national symbol is the black panther — a rare melanistic big cat — making it one of the only nations in the world to choose this elusive animal as its primary national emblem.

This country exports ships as its second-largest commodity by value alongside crude petroleum and manganese ore — an unusual maritime export for a small equatorial African nation with a population of only 2.5 million.

This country's natural resources include niobium and uranium alongside petroleum, manganese, and gold — a combination of rare strategic metals and conventional energy resources found together in very few other Central African nations.

This country achieves a GDP per capita of $18,900 — among the highest in sub-Saharan Africa — despite a small population of 2.5 million, with petroleum revenues generating prosperity described as making it one of the most stable nations on the continent.

name: United Kingdom
funFacts: This country is the only nation to have voluntarily left the European Union, doing so on 31 January 2020 in a process known as 'Brexit,' following a 2016 referendum in which 52% of voters chose to leave.

This country does not celebrate a single national holiday — uniquely among European nations, it has no official day marking its founding, unification, or independence, because it came together through a gradual process of Acts of Union spanning centuries.

This country's overseas territories include Caribbean islands, and its highest point, Mount Scenery at 862 m on the island of Saba, is located in the Caribbean Sea — meaning the tallest point associated with this country is thousands of miles from its mainland.

This country has a coastline of 12,429 km and only one land border — with Ireland — making it effectively an island nation, and it was historically the world's leading sea power, with the British Empire at its peak covering one-fourth of the Earth's surface.

This country's national symbols vary by constituent nation: a lion and Tudor rose for England, a thistle and unicorn for Scotland, a dragon and daffodil for Wales, and a shamrock and flax for Northern Ireland — reflecting that it is a union of distinct nations each with its own identity.

name: Georgia
funFacts: This country's native name 'Sak'art'velo' means 'Land of the Kartvelians,' while the Western name 'Georgia' derives from the people called the Gurz — two completely different etymologies for the same nation depending on which language you use.

This country exports wine as one of its top five commodities — one of the only Caucasian nations where wine appears in official export data — reflecting one of the world's oldest continuous winemaking traditions in its highland valleys.

This country exports cars as its single largest commodity alongside copper ore and electricity — automobiles (largely re-exported transit vehicles) ranking above traditional Caucasian mining and energy products.

This country's national symbol is Saint George — the same patron saint of England — giving two countries on opposite ends of the Eurasian continent the exact same historical and religious figure as their primary national emblem.

This country's highest point, Mt'a Shkhara at 5,193 meters, rises from the Greater Caucasus range along its northern border — a glaciated summit at the frontier between Europe and Asia that stands taller than Mont Blanc.

name: Ghana
funFacts: This country gained independence from the United Kingdom on 6 March 1957 — the first sub-Saharan African nation to achieve independence from a European colonial power in the post-World War II era.

This country's name derives from a historical tribal chieftain whose actual territory lay northwest of where the modern country sits — one of the few nations named after a historical figure whose domain did not overlap its current borders.

This country exports cocoa beans and cocoa paste as two separate top-five export commodities alongside gold — reflecting a vertically integrated cocoa industry that produces both raw beans and processed cocoa products for export.

This country sends 24% of its exports to Switzerland and 18% to the UAE — both known as major gold trading hubs — with nearly half of all exports flowing to two non-neighboring gold markets on different continents.

This country's natural resources include bauxite, manganese, industrial diamonds, and petroleum alongside gold and rubber — one of the most diversified mineral and natural resource profiles among West African coastal nations.

name: Guinea
funFacts: This country sends 50% of its exports to the UAE and 36% to China — with 86% going to just two buyers — making it one of the most export-concentrated African economies, shipping gold and aluminum ore almost exclusively to Gulf and Asian markets.

This country's natural resources include bauxite, iron ore, diamonds, and gold — four distinct valuable minerals — giving it one of the richest mineral endowments in West Africa despite a GDP per capita of only $4,000.

This country borders six nations — Cote d'Ivoire, Guinea-Bissau, Liberia, Mali, Senegal, and Sierra Leone — more land neighbors than any other coastal West African country, reflecting its central position in the region.

This country gained independence from France on 2 October 1958 — earlier than most French African colonies — by voting to sever all ties with France, making it the first French sub-Saharan territory to choose complete independence over continued association.

This country exports aluminum ore as its second-largest commodity — reflecting extensive bauxite deposits from which aluminum is refined — yet sends the raw ore abroad rather than processing it domestically into finished metal.

name: The Gambia
funFacts: This country sends 92% of its exports to Kazakhstan — an extraordinarily concentrated trade relationship between one of Africa's smallest nations and a Central Asian country thousands of kilometers away.

This country's exports consist of packaged medicine, cars, harvesting machinery, refined petroleum, and trailers — none produced domestically in significant quantities, reflecting an economy built almost entirely on transit and re-export trade.

This country's highest point is an unnamed elevation at just 63 meters — one of the lowest national high points in the entire world, with terrain so flat the country sits almost entirely at near-sea-level elevations.

This country is bordered on three sides by Senegal — with which it once formed a short-lived confederation — leaving only its short Atlantic coast as its escape from near-complete encirclement by a single neighbor.
This country's total area of 11,300 square kilometers makes it the smallest mainland nation in Africa — a narrow strip of land on either bank of the Gambia River, flanked almost entirely by Senegal.

name: Guinea-Bissau
funFacts: This country sends 66% of its exports to India — primarily cashews — one of the most India-dependent African economies and a major supplier of cashew nuts to the world's largest cashew-consuming nation.

This country's highest point, Dongol Ronde at only 277 meters, is among the lowest national high points in Africa — terrain so flat and low that the country sits almost entirely at coastal and near-coastal elevations.
This country declared independence on 24 September 1973 — over a year before Portugal formally recognized it on 10 September 1974 — celebrating independence before the colonial power acknowledged it.
This country borders only two nations — Guinea and Senegal — making it one of the least-bordered countries on the African mainland, despite sitting on the Atlantic coast of a densely bordered region.

This country's top five exports are cashews, fish, fish oil, processed crustaceans, and malt extract — an almost entirely seafood and nut-based export economy with no petroleum, gold, or industrial minerals in its top commodities.

name: Equatorial Guinea
funFacts: This country is one of the few African nations colonized by Spain rather than France or Britain, gaining independence on 12 October 1968 — the same date as Spain's own National Day — a colonial coincidence embedded in its founding moment.

This country's national symbol is the silk cotton tree — one of the only African nations to use a tree rather than an animal as its primary national symbol — reflecting the dense tropical forests of both its island and mainland territories.

This country's capital, Malabo, sits on the island of Bioko in the Gulf of Guinea — entirely separate from the mainland portion of the country — meaning the seat of government is on a different landmass from most of the national territory.

This country exports alcohols as its third-largest commodity alongside crude petroleum and natural gas — one of the few oil-producing African nations to list processed alcohols among its top five exports.

This country borders only two mainland nations — Cameroon and Gabon — yet also controls the island of Bioko where its capital sits, giving it a uniquely bifurcated geographic identity as both a mainland and island state.

name: Greece
funFacts: This country's official name is the Hellenic Republic, not 'Greece' — the name 'Greece' derives from the Roman term Graecia, while Greeks call their own country Ellas or Ellada, tracing back to the mythological figure Hellen.

This country has a coastline of 13,676 km — the longest in the Mediterranean and the 11th longest in the world — driven by its enormous archipelago of over 6,000 islands, of which around 230 are inhabited.

This country exports olive oil and tobacco alongside refined petroleum and packaged medicine, and is the world's third-largest olive oil producer, a crop that has been central to its economy and cuisine since antiquity.

This country suffered one of the most severe debt crises in modern European history between 2009 and 2019, entering three consecutive international bailout agreements totaling approximately $300 billion before exiting the EU's enhanced financial surveillance framework.

This country is the birthplace of democracy, the Olympics, and Western philosophy, and its capital Athens houses the Acropolis — one of the most visited ancient monuments in the world — on a hill overlooking a modern metropolis of over 3 million people.

name: Grenada
funFacts: This country is the world's second-largest producer of nutmeg, and nutmeg and cardamom are its leading export commodity — earning it the nickname 'Isle of Spice.'
This country gained independence on 7 February 1974 and was the site of a US military intervention in 1983 after an internal coup overthrew and killed Prime Minister Maurice Bishop.
This country's highest point is Mount Saint Catherine at 840 m, its coastline is 121 km, and its total area is 344 sq km — roughly twice the size of Washington, D.C.
This country's name likely derives from the Spanish city of Granada; in Spanish, 'granada' means 'pomegranate.'
This country's national symbols are the Grenada dove and the bougainvillea flower, and its capital is Saint George's.

name: Guatemala
funFacts: This country is home to Volcan Tajumulco, the highest point in all of Central America at 4,220 m above sea level.

This country's top exports are garments, bananas, coffee, palm oil, and raw sugar — with coffee being a distinctive agricultural export that sets it apart from purely industrial exporters in the region.
This country's name derives from the Nahuatl word 'Quauhtemallan,' meaning 'land of the eagle,' as interpreted by Spanish conquistadors' Mexican allies.

This country's national bird is the quetzal, which also gives its name to the national currency, and over 41% of its population identifies as Maya — the highest proportion of any Central American nation.
This country gained independence from Spain on 15 September 1821 and endured a 36-year guerrilla war that ended with a peace agreement in 1996.

name: Guyana
funFacts: This country's GDP per capita of $70,300 is the highest in South America — a dramatic rise driven by offshore crude petroleum discoveries that transformed it from one of the region's poorest to one of its wealthiest nations.
This country was the only mainland South American nation colonized by Britain rather than Spain or Portugal, gaining independence from the United Kingdom on 26 May 1966.

This country's highest point, Laberintos del Norte on Mount Roraima at 2,775 meters, sits at the tri-border junction with Venezuela and Brazil — a towering tabletop mountain whose sheer cliffs rise from surrounding jungle.

This country's national symbols include three distinct elements — the Canje pheasant (hoatzin), the jaguar, and the Victoria Regia water lily — reflecting the biodiversity of its Amazon-adjacent lowland ecosystems.

This country exports crude petroleum, railway cargo containers, gold, ships, and rice — a strikingly diverse commodity list that includes both industrial containers and precious metal within its top five exports.

name: Honduras
funFacts: This country's name means 'depths' in Spanish, referring to the deep anchorage in the northern Bay of Trujillo.
