This country's national symbols are the scarlet macaw and the white-tailed deer, and its top exports are garments, coffee, insulated wire, palm oil, and shellfish.

This country has a coastline of 823 km split between the Caribbean Sea (669 km) and the Gulf of Fonseca (163 km) on the Pacific side — one of only two nations in this region with coasts on both oceans.
This country's highest point is Cerro Las Minas at 2,870 m, and Hurricane Mitch devastated it in 1998, killing about 5,600 people and causing approximately $2 billion in damage.
This country borders Guatemala, El Salvador, and Nicaragua, and the USA receives 49% of its exports — the highest trade concentration of any mainland Central American nation.

name: Croatia
funFacts: This country has a coastline of 5,835 km — the vast majority of which (4,058 km) consists of islands rather than mainland shore — giving it one of the most island-studded Adriatic fronts in Europe.
This country's national symbol is the red-and-white checkerboard pattern, one of the oldest heraldic designs in Europe, traceable to the medieval Croatian Kingdom and now displayed on its flag.

This country was the final EU member to join both the Eurozone and Schengen Area simultaneously, completing both transitions in January 2023, making it among the most recently fully integrated EU states.
This country exports ships as its top commodity, reflecting a centuries-old Adriatic shipbuilding tradition, alongside garments and electricity.

This country declared independence from Yugoslavia in 1991 but fought a four-year war before Yugoslav forces were fully cleared from its territory; the last Serb-held enclave in eastern Slavonia was returned only in 1998 under UN supervision.

name: Haiti
funFacts: This country declared independence on 1 January 1804, becoming the first country in the world to be led by formerly enslaved people after a successful revolution against French colonial rule.
This country is the poorest nation in the Western Hemisphere, with a GDP per capita of $2,800 (2024 est.), and French and Haitian Creole are both official languages.
This country's name derives from the Arawak word 'Ayti,' meaning 'Land of Mountains,' originally applied to the entire island of Hispaniola.
This country's highest point is Pic la Selle at 2,674 m, and it was forced to pay France an indemnity of 100 million francs for over a century following its independence.
This country exports essential oils as one of its top commodities alongside garments, scrap iron, and bedding, with 82% of its exports going to the USA.

name: Hungary
funFacts: This country's name in its own language, Magyarorszag, means 'Country of the Magyars' — a reference to the dominant Finno-Ugric tribe that arrived from the Eurasian steppe in the 9th century, making Hungarians linguistically unrelated to all their Slavic, Germanic, and Romance-speaking neighbors.
This country is landlocked and surrounded by seven nations — Austria, Croatia, Romania, Serbia, Slovakia, Slovenia, and Ukraine — one of the highest neighbor-counts for a landlocked European state.

This country developed what became known as 'Goulash Communism' under leader Janos Kadar in 1968, an early experiment in liberalizing a Soviet-bloc economy that gave Hungary a more market-oriented system than other Warsaw Pact states decades before the Iron Curtain fell.

This country exports electric batteries as one of its top commodities alongside cars and vehicle parts — reflecting its emergence as a major site for electric vehicle battery manufacturing, driven by large investments from Asian automakers.

This country's national symbol is the Holy Crown of Saint Stephen, also called the Crown of Hungary, which has been a sacred object of national identity for over a thousand years and is displayed in the Hungarian Parliament building.

name: Indonesia
funFacts: This country's coastline of 54,716 kilometers is one of the longest in the world — reflecting its status as Earth's largest archipelago nation — its thousands of islands stretching across the Indian and Pacific Oceans between mainland Southeast Asia and Australia.

This country's national symbol is the garuda — a mythical bird from Hindu-Buddhist mythology — making it the most populous Muslim-majority nation in the world whose primary national symbol is drawn from pre-Islamic Hindu-Buddhist religious tradition.

This country exports palm oil alongside coal, lignite, and iron alloys — one of the few nations whose top-five exports combine a tropical agricultural commodity with industrial minerals — reflecting its dual identity as both a major agricultural and extractive economy.

This country borders only three nations — Malaysia, Papua New Guinea, and Timor-Leste — despite its archipelago spanning over 17,000 islands, because the vast majority of its island territory shares no land with any other country.

This country declared independence on 17 August 1945 from the Netherlands — within days of Japan's World War II surrender — making its independence declaration one of the most strategically timed in Asian history, seizing the window before Dutch colonial control could be reimposed.

name: India
funFacts: This country's coal reserves are described as the fourth-largest in the world — a resource superlative rarely cited for South Asian nations — alongside diamonds listed as a named natural resource, giving it the unusual combination of a precious gemstone and a globally significant fossil fuel reserve.

This country exports packaged medicine as one of its top five commodities alongside refined petroleum, diamonds, and broadcasting equipment — one of the few Asian nations where pharmaceutical products appear in the top-five export list, reflecting a globally significant generic drug manufacturing industry.

This country's official national symbol is the Lion Capital of Ashoka — an ancient sculpted emblem depicting four Asiatic lions standing back-to-back on a circular abacus, carved in the 3rd century B.C. — a modern nation whose primary official emblem is drawn directly from a Buddhist archaeological monument.

This country's highest point is Kanchenjunga at 8,586 meters rather than Mount Everest — because Everest's summit is attributed to Nepal — making Kanchenjunga, the world's third-highest peak, the tallest terrain that sits within its own borders.

This country borders six nations — Bangladesh, Bhutan, Burma, China, Nepal, and Pakistan — more land neighbors than any other South Asian country except China, reflecting its position as the geographic center of the entire South Asian subcontinent.

name: Ireland
funFacts: This country has a GDP per capita of $115,300 — the second highest in the EU — driven largely by multinational pharmaceutical and technology companies that have made it Europe's leading exporter of vaccines, packaged medicine, nitrogen compounds, and integrated circuits.
This country is the only English-speaking nation in the eurozone and one of only two countries in the world to have Irish (Gaelic) as its first official language, alongside English.

This country experienced a catastrophic famine in the mid-19th century that caused an almost 25% decline in the island's population through starvation, disease, and emigration — a demographic trauma so severe that its total population did not recover to pre-famine levels until the late 20th century.

This country shares its only land border with the United Kingdom (Northern Ireland), a relationship governed by the 1998 Belfast/Good Friday Agreement, which ended decades of sectarian conflict known as the Troubles.

This country maintains a policy of military neutrality — it did not participate in World War II and has never joined NATO — while remaining a full EU member, a combination unique among Western European states of comparable size.

name: Iran
funFacts: This country's name derives from the Sanskrit word 'arya' meaning 'people of the mountainous land' — the etymological root of the term 'Aryan' — and replaced the Western name 'Persia' when the country formally requested the change.

This country's highest point, Kuh-e Damavand at 5,625 meters, is a dormant stratovolcano — making it the highest volcanic peak in Asia and one of the highest national summits in the entire Middle East and Central Asian region.
This country exports alcohols as one of its top five commodities alongside natural gas and refined copper — industrial-grade alcohols representing a significant petrochemical manufacturing output.

This country borders seven nations — Afghanistan, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Iraq, Pakistan, Turkey, and Turkmenistan — more than any other Middle Eastern country, reflecting its position at the crossroads of the Arab world, the Caucasus, and South and Central Asia.

This country's republic was proclaimed on 1 April 1979, yet its factbook notes an Achaemenid (Persian) Empire established around 550 B.C. — situating its modern Islamic Republic within one of the world's oldest continuous state traditions.

name: Iraq
funFacts: This country's name probably derives from Uruk, the ancient Sumerian and Babylonian city on the Euphrates River — one of history's earliest urban centers — giving a modern nation its name from a settlement that flourished over 5,000 years ago.

This country has only 58 kilometers of coastline on the Persian Gulf — the shortest ocean access of any Gulf-bordering nation — a narrow strip reflecting how borders were drawn in the region after the First World War.

This country's top five exports consist almost entirely of petroleum products — crude petroleum, refined petroleum, petroleum coke, and natural gas — plus gold, making it one of the most hydrocarbon-concentrated export economies in the world.
This country sends 33% of its exports to China and 28% to India — with over 60% flowing to two Asian buyers — a trade concentration driven by Asian demand for its crude petroleum.

This country celebrates two national holidays: Independence Day on 3 October 1932 (from British mandate) and Republic Day on 14 July 1958 (the military coup ending the monarchy) — treating both colonial liberation and regime change as founding national moments.

name: Iceland
funFacts: This country hosts the world's oldest functioning parliament, the Althingi, which was established in 930 A.D. — nearly a century before England's Parliament and over 800 years before most modern democratic legislatures.

This country has no land borders with any other nation, sits entirely on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, and generates most of its electricity from geothermal and hydropower — making it one of the world's most volcanically active and renewably powered societies.

This country exports aluminum as its top commodity despite having no bauxite deposits — it imports aluminum oxide and smelts it using abundant geothermal and hydropower, creating an energy-for-metal industrial model unique in Europe.

This country's population is around 364,000, making it the most sparsely populated country in Europe, yet it has a GDP per capita of $65,600 — one of the highest in the world — driven by tourism, fisheries, and aluminum.

This country lost 20% of its population to emigration in the decades following the 1875 eruption of the Askja volcano, which devastated its economy; today it faces the opposite challenge, managing a rapid tourism and construction boom.

name: Israel
funFacts: This country's lowest point, the Dead Sea at -431 meters below sea level, is the deepest exposed land surface in the factbook dataset — a hypersaline lake too salty for aquatic life, shared with neighboring Jordan.

This country exports integrated circuits and medical instruments as its top export commodities alongside diamonds — combining semiconductor manufacturing with precision medical devices in a high-technology profile unlike any other Middle Eastern nation.

This country's natural resources include magnesium bromide — a highly specific industrial chemical used in drilling fluids and pharmaceuticals — alongside potash and phosphate rock, a precise mineral combination found in very few other nations' resource lists.

This country's industries encompass aviation, communications, computer-aided design, medical electronics, and fiber optics — one of the most concentrated high-technology industrial descriptions of any nation in the Middle East.

This country's national symbols are the Star of David and the menorah — both ancient Jewish religious artifacts — making it one of the few modern nations where official national symbols are drawn directly from religious iconography rather than animals or landscapes.

name: Italy
funFacts: This country encloses two independent states within its own territory — the Vatican City and San Marino — a distinction no other country on Earth holds, making it the only nation that is the sovereign neighbor of two micro-states simultaneously.

This country's highest point is listed as Mont Blanc de Courmayeur at 4,748 m — a secondary summit of Mont Blanc — because the two countries dispute which side of the peak marks the true summit; France claims 4,810 m on its side.

This country exports packaged medicine as its single largest commodity, outpacing its famous garments, cars, and food products — reflecting decades of pharmaceutical industry growth that has made it one of Europe's leading medicine manufacturers.

This country became a unified nation-state only in 1861, one of the last major European nations to do so, having previously existed as a patchwork of city-states, papal territories, kingdoms, and foreign-controlled regions for centuries.

This country's name may derive from a word meaning 'calf' — linked to the Latin vitulus — according to one of the leading etymological theories, with the name originally applied to a tribe in what is now Calabria before spreading to the whole peninsula.

name: Jamaica
funFacts: This country's name comes from the Arawak word 'xaymaca,' meaning 'Land of Wood and Water' or possibly 'Land of Springs.'
This country is the leading Caribbean exporter of aluminum oxide (alumina), which ranks as its top export commodity, derived from its significant bauxite deposits.
This country's national bird is the green-and-black streamertail, a hummingbird species endemic to the island, and its highest point is Blue Mountain Peak at 2,256 m.
This country gained independence on 6 August 1962 and was previously part of the short-lived Federation of the West Indies (1958–1962) before withdrawing to pursue independence separately.
This country's capital is Kingston, and the Rastafarian religious movement — which originated here — accounts for 1.1% of the population according to 2011 census data.

name: Jordan
funFacts: This country has only 26 kilometers of coastline — all of it on a single narrow inlet of the Red Sea at the port of Aqaba — giving it one of the shortest ocean frontages of any coastal nation in the world.

This country exports fertilizers, phosphates, and phosphoric acid among its top five commodities — making phosphate-derived chemicals the backbone of its export economy, fundamentally different from the petroleum-dominant exports of every Gulf neighbor.

This country shares the Dead Sea at -431 meters with Israel as its lowest point — the deepest exposed land surface in the factbook dataset — yet its national territory rises to 1,854 meters at its highest point.

This country sends 21% of its exports to the USA — a higher share to the United States than most other Middle Eastern nations — reflecting a significant trade relationship in garments and pharmaceuticals.

This country's natural resources are listed as only phosphates, potash, and shale oil — one of the sparsest resource profiles in the Middle East — making its phosphate chemical industry central to an economy with very limited oil and gas.

name: Japan
funFacts: This country's natural resources are listed as 'negligible mineral resources' and fish — the sparsest resource profile of any major East Asian economy — yet achieves a GDP per capita of $46,100 through a manufacturing and technology economy built almost entirely on imported raw materials.

This country has no land borders — an island nation with zero border countries in its factbook entry — yet its 29,751-kilometer coastline touches the Pacific Ocean, Sea of Japan, and East China Sea, placing it within maritime reach of Korea, China, and Russia.

This country's independence factbook entry lists 11 February 660 B.C. as a notable earlier date — a mythological founding by Emperor Jimmu — giving it one of the most ancient founding dates recorded in any nation's factbook, predating most modern civilizations.

This country exports cars, integrated circuits, machinery, vehicle parts, and construction vehicles — a top-five export list composed entirely of manufactured machinery and vehicles with no agricultural goods, raw materials, or unprocessed commodities.

This country's national symbols are the red sun disc and the chrysanthemum — the sun disc appearing on its flag as a direct symbol of its national identity and the chrysanthemum serving as the imperial seal — two distinct emblems representing the nation and its ancient dynasty respectively.

name: Kazakhstan
funFacts: This country's highest point, Pik Khan-Tengri at 7,010 meters, is noted as the northernmost 7,000-meter peak in the world — a geographic superlative making it unique among the high summits of Central Asia.

This country exports radioactive chemicals among its top five commodities alongside crude petroleum, gold, and refined copper — one of the very few nations in the world to list radioactive chemicals as a formal top-five export, reflecting its role as a major uranium producer.
This country's area of 2,724,900 square kilometers makes it the world's largest landlocked nation — a territory spanning from the Caspian Sea in the west to the Altai Mountains in the east.

This country's GDP per capita of $35,900 is the highest in Central Asia — generated from a diverse extraction economy encompassing petroleum, coal, uranium, copper, gold, and iron ore alongside agricultural machinery production.

This country's natural resources include uranium alongside major deposits of petroleum, natural gas, coal, iron ore, manganese, copper, molybdenum, lead, zinc, and gold — one of the most mineralogically diverse resource profiles of any former Soviet republic.

name: Kenya
funFacts: This country is named after its highest peak, Mount Kenya at 5,199 meters — whose name derives from the Kikuyu phrase 'kere nyaga,' meaning 'white mountain,' referring to its glaciated summit.

This country exports tea, cut flowers, and tropical fruits among its top five commodities — a combination of warm-climate agricultural products that reflects both highland tea estates and a major horticultural export industry.
This country's top two export markets are Uganda and the USA at 10% each — an unusual parity between a neighboring African country and the world's largest economy as co-equal trading partners.

This country borders five nations — Ethiopia, Somalia, South Sudan, Tanzania, and Uganda — while maintaining a coastline on the Indian Ocean, making it a critical hub connecting East Africa's landlocked interior to maritime trade routes.

This country's natural resources include fluorspar — a mineral used in steel production and fluorine chemistry — alongside soda ash and gemstones, industrial and precious minerals that rarely appear together in a single East African nation's resource profile.

name: Kyrgyzstan
funFacts: This country sends 30% of its exports to Switzerland — the highest share to a single buyer among its top partners — with gold as its dominant commodity, reflecting the Swiss precious metals trading infrastructure as the primary destination for its mined output.

This country's natural resources explicitly list rare earth metals alongside hydropower and gold — one of the few Central Asian nations to formally include rare earth minerals as a named resource, reflecting deposits of materials critical to modern electronics manufacturing.

This country's highest point, Jengish Chokusu (Pik Pobedy) at 7,439 meters, rises from the Tian Shan range on its border with China — one of the highest national summits in Central Asia and the highest in the entire Kyrgyz mountain system.

This country's national symbol is the white falcon — a bird of prey that reflects its ancient nomadic pastoral culture — distinguishing it from neighbors whose symbols are horses, eagles, or mythological creatures.

This country exports garments among its top five commodities alongside gold and coal — the only Central Asian nation to include a manufactured textile product in its top-five export list — reflecting a developing light manufacturing sector alongside its dominant mining economy.

name: Cambodia
funFacts: This country's national symbols are Angkor Wat — a 12th-century temple complex considered one of the world's greatest architectural achievements — and the kouprey, a wild ox considered among the rarest large mammals on Earth — making its national symbols a pairing of architectural heritage and a critically endangered animal.

This country sends 36% of its exports to the United States — the highest share to the US among all Southeast Asian nations — primarily garments produced in its export-oriented textile manufacturing sector.

This country exports semiconductors as a top-five commodity alongside garments, trunks, and footwear — one of the few developing-economy Southeast Asian nations to have semiconductor components appear in its top-five exports alongside labor-intensive manufactured goods.

This country's natural resources include gemstones alongside oil and gas, timber, iron ore, manganese, and phosphates — reflecting a resource base that spans precious minerals alongside conventional energy and industrial materials.

This country gained independence on 9 November 1953 from France — making it one of the last Southeast Asian nations to achieve independence from European colonial rule — at a time when the broader region was undergoing rapid decolonization.

name: Kiribati
funFacts: This country's natural resources note that phosphate production was discontinued in 1979 — after the deposits on Banaba Island were completely exhausted — leaving fish and coconut products as its only remaining resources and marking one of the few factbook entries to document a resource's full depletion.

This country sends 85% of its exports to Thailand — the highest concentration to a single buyer among Pacific Island nations — almost entirely fish, making it one of the most trade-concentrated micro-nations in the entire factbook dataset.

This country's top exports are listed as only fish and coconut oil — the most minimal top-five export list of any sovereign nation in the factbook — an economy reduced to two commodities after the exhaustion of its once-significant phosphate deposits.

This country's national symbol is the frigatebird — a seabird with one of the largest wingspan-to-body-weight ratios of any bird — shared as a national symbol with Nauru, making two Pacific Island nations use the same seabird as their primary national emblem.

This country's area of 811 square kilometers is spread across 33 atolls in three island groups spanning a vast expanse of the central Pacific Ocean — its territory distributed across one of the widest geographic footprints relative to land area of any sovereign nation.

name: Saint Kitts and Nevis
funFacts: This country is the smallest sovereign state in the Western Hemisphere by both area (261 sq km) and population (55,434), consisting of two islands separated by just 3 km of water.

This country gained independence on 19 September 1983, the last British Caribbean territory to do so in the 20th century, and held a referendum in 1998 in which the island of Nevis narrowly failed to secede.

This country's name partly derives from Christopher Columbus, who named the larger island after his own patron saint; 'Kitt' was a common nickname for Christopher, while 'Nevis' comes from the Spanish 'Las Nieves' (The Snows), referring to its cloud-capped mountain.

This country's highest point is Mount Liamuiga at 1,156 m on Saint Kitts, a dormant volcano, and at the turn of the 18th century it was the richest British Crown Colony per capita in the Caribbean due to the sugar trade.
This country exports ships and beer as its top commodities, with Malta receiving 49% of its exports — an unusual trade relationship for a small Caribbean island nation.

name: South Korea
funFacts: This country's only land border is with North Korea — making it a peninsula that effectively functions as an island for overland travel and trade — its southern, western, and eastern coastlines bounded by the Korea Strait, Yellow Sea, and Sea of Japan.

This country's national symbols include the taegeuk (yin-yang symbol), the Rose of Sharon (Hibiscus syriacus), and the Siberian tiger — one of the most diverse official national symbol sets in East Asia, combining a philosophical diagram, a flowering plant, and a large predatory mammal.

This country's GDP per capita of $50,400 is the highest in mainland East Asia — a level achieved within a single generation through industrialization centered on electronics, automobiles, and shipbuilding that transformed a war-devastated economy.

This country exports integrated circuits as its top commodity alongside cars, refined petroleum, and plastics — a diversified high-technology export profile combining semiconductors, automotive manufacturing, and petrochemical products in a single top-five list.

This country gained independence on 15 August 1945 from Japan — the same date as North Korea's independence — giving the two Korean states, which share an ethnicity, language, and pre-division history, identical independence dates despite decades of political separation.

name: Kuwait
funFacts: This country's name derives from the Arabic 'al-kuwayt,' from the Hindustani word 'kut' meaning a fortress-like structure near water — a name given to the coastal fort that preceded the modern city and nation.

This country's entire top-five export list consists of crude petroleum, refined petroleum, natural gas, hydrocarbons, and plastics — making it one of the most hydrocarbon-concentrated export economies in the world, with no non-petroleum commodity in its top five.
This country borders only two nations — Iraq and Saudi Arabia — making it the Gulf state with the fewest land neighbors, its territory wedged between two much larger countries.

This country's natural resources are listed as only petroleum, fish, shrimp, and natural gas — yet its GDP per capita of $45,400 reflects the extreme wealth generated by one of the world's most concentrated oil reserves relative to population.

This country's highest point reaches only 300 meters — an unnamed location near its border post — making it the Middle Eastern nation with the lowest national high point, a country so flat that even its highest terrain is barely a hill.

name: Laos
funFacts: This country exports electricity as its top commodity — a landlocked Southeast Asian nation whose primary export by value is electrical power generated from Mekong River dams and sold to neighboring Thailand and China — an energy-as-export model rare among developing landlocked nations.

This country sends 39% of exports to China and 34% to Thailand — 73% to just two neighbors — one of the highest bilateral trade concentrations in Southeast Asia, driven by electricity and fertilizer sales to adjacent buyers.

This country borders five nations — Burma, Cambodia, China, Thailand, and Vietnam — more land neighbors than any other Southeast Asian nation, reflecting its position as the geographic heart of mainland Southeast Asia despite being one of the region's smaller landlocked countries.

This country's national symbol is the elephant — a living terrestrial animal — distinguishing it from Southeast Asian neighbors whose primary symbols are mythological creatures such as the garuda (Indonesia, Thailand) or chinthe (Burma).

This country has two recognized independence dates: 19 July 1949 (from France) and 22 October 1953 (when the Franco-Lao Treaty recognized full independence) — a four-year gap between partial and complete sovereignty noted explicitly in its factbook entry.

name: Lebanon
funFacts: This country's name derives from the Semitic root 'lbn,' meaning 'white,' referring to its snow-capped mountains — one of the few countries in the Middle East named not for its people or a river but for the snow on its terrain.
This country's national symbol is the cedar tree — an ancient species that appears on its national flag and has been used in the region's iconography since antiquity.

This country exports jewelry, cars, diamonds, and gold among its top five commodities — a predominantly precious goods and re-export profile with no petroleum, industrial machinery, or agricultural products in its top five.
This country's industries include wine production — listing winemaking alongside banking and tourism — one of the only Arab nations to formally list wine as a named industrial sector.

This country's tiny area of 10,400 square kilometers borders only Israel and Syria, yet its Mediterranean coastline gives it access to European trade routes that made Beirut a major regional commercial hub for centuries.

name: Liberia
funFacts: This country's name derives from the Latin word 'liber,' meaning 'free,' because it was established in the 19th century as a homeland for liberated African-American slaves — one of the few nations whose name literally encodes its founding purpose.
This country declared independence on 26 July 1847 — predating most African nations' independence by over a century — making it one of the oldest continuously independent republics on the continent.

This country is described as one of the most ethnically diverse in the world, with 28 ethnic groups and languages — a mosaic of West African peoples alongside the Americo-Liberian descendants of freed slaves who founded the nation.

This country sends 30% of its exports to Switzerland — primarily gold — making it one of West Africa's most Switzerland-dependent economies, with gold as the primary export for a country with a GDP per capita of only $1,700.

This country exports ships as its second-largest commodity alongside gold and iron ore — an unusual maritime asset export for a West African nation, reflecting its historical role as a registry for international shipping vessels.

name: Libya
funFacts: This country's natural resources are listed as only petroleum, natural gas, and gypsum — one of the sparsest mineral profiles for such a large desert nation — reflecting that most of its 1,759,540 square kilometers are covered by the Sahara.

This country's national holiday is Liberation Day on 23 October 2011 — the date marking the end of its civil war — rather than its formal independence date of 1951, reflecting that the recent revolution is treated as the more defining national moment.

This country's name derives from the Libu, a North African tribe first documented in ancient texts from the 13th century B.C. — one of the oldest attested ethnic names that survives directly in a modern country name.
This country's national anthem is titled 'Libya, Libya, Libya' — one of the few national anthems in the world where the entire title consists solely of the country's own name repeated three times.

This country exports crude petroleum primarily to Italy (23%) and Germany (15%) — with Western European nations receiving the majority of its oil — reflecting a Mediterranean energy trade relationship concentrated among a small set of European buyers.

name: Saint Lucia
funFacts: This country is believed to have been named after Saint Lucy of Syracuse by French sailors shipwrecked there on 13 December 1502 — her feast day — making it one of the few countries named after a woman.
This country's national symbols are the twin Piton volcanic peaks and the Saint Lucia parrot, an endemic species found nowhere else in the world.
This country changed hands between England and France 14 times before being finally ceded to the UK in 1814, the most disputed colonial possession in Caribbean history.
This country gained independence on 22 February 1979, and its top exports are refined petroleum and gravel and crushed stone, with Guyana receiving 20% of its exports.

This country has a highest point of Mount Gimie at 948 m and a total area of 616 sq km, roughly 3.5 times the size of Washington, D.C., making it notably larger than most of its Eastern Caribbean island neighbors.

name: Liechtenstein
funFacts: This country is one of only two doubly landlocked nations in the world — surrounded entirely by other landlocked countries (Austria and Switzerland) — and is the smallest doubly landlocked state on Earth.
This country has a GDP per capita of over $210,000, making it one of the wealthiest countries on Earth by that measure, driven by its low-tax financial system and precision manufacturing industries.

This country takes its name from the House of Liechtenstein, a noble family that purchased and united the counties of Schellenburg and Vaduz in 1719; the family name itself comes from an Austrian castle meaning 'light stone' in German.

This country entered a customs and monetary union with Switzerland after World War I when its own economy was devastated — meaning it uses the Swiss franc and has essentially outsourced its border controls to its neighbor.

This country exports specialty goods including dental products, connectors for audio and video equipment, and precision instruments, yet has an urbanization rate of only about 14.6% — the lowest in Western Europe.

name: Sri Lanka
funFacts: This country has no land borders — its factbook lists zero border countries — an island nation in the Indian Ocean whose geographic isolation did not prevent Colombo from becoming one of South Asia's most historically significant maritime trading ports.

This country has two distinct capitals: Colombo serving as the commercial capital and Sri Jayewardenepura Kotte as the legislative capital — one of the few nations in South Asia where governmental functions are formally split between two separate cities.

This country exports used rubber tires as a top-five commodity alongside garments, tea, precious stones, and rubber products — one of the only nations in the world where processed scrap rubber appears in the top-five export list as a significant standalone commodity.

This country's natural resources include graphite alongside gems and mineral sands — natural graphite being a strategic industrial mineral used in batteries and lubricants that appears in no other South Asian nation's resource inventory.

This country exports tea as a top-five commodity alongside precious stones — a combination of a plantation agricultural commodity and gemstones that distinguishes its export profile from every other South Asian nation, none of which lists both tea and precious stones in their top five.

name: Lesotho
funFacts: This country is the only nation in the world whose borders are entirely encircled by a single other country — South Africa — making it one of the most geographically unusual sovereign states on Earth.

This country's lowest point, the junction of the Orange and Makhaleng Rivers at 1,400 meters above sea level, sits higher than the national high points of many other countries — reflecting that its entire territory occupies elevated highland terrain.

This country's national symbol is the mokorotio, a traditional woven Basotho hat — one of the only African nations to choose a cultural artifact rather than an animal or plant as its primary national emblem.

This country exports diamonds, garments, wool, and bedding — a distinctive mix of precious stones and textile products that reflects both its diamond-bearing geology and its tradition of highland sheep farming.

This country's name comes from the Sotho people, whose name means 'dark-skinned,' with the prefix 'Le-' indicating singular form — while its former colonial name, Basutoland, used the plural 'Ba-' prefix for 'people.'

name: Lithuania
funFacts: This country was the first Soviet republic to declare independence from the USSR, doing so on 11 March 1990 — over a year before the Soviet Union formally dissolved.
This country's medieval Grand Duchy was, by the end of the 14th century, the largest state in Europe, stretching from the Baltic Sea deep into what is now Ukraine and Belarus.

This country borders the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad to its west — a landlocked sliver of Russian territory on the Baltic coast that can only be reached from Russia by crossing this country or other NATO members.

This country's natural resources are notably modest, listed as peat, arable land, and amber — making amber one of its few distinct raw materials, fitting for a nation that has been a center of amber trade since ancient times.

This country exports refined petroleum, furniture, and plastic products as its top commodities, despite importing all of its crude petroleum — reflecting its role as a petroleum-processing hub rather than a producer.

name: Luxembourg
funFacts: This country is officially a Grand Duchy — the world's only remaining sovereign Grand Duchy — and celebrates its national day on the birthday of Grand Duke Henri rather than an independence date.

This country was one of the six founding members of the European Economic Community in 1957, and its capital city hosts several major EU institutions, including the Court of Justice of the European Union.
This country gained its full independence in 1867 by agreeing to permanent neutrality, but that neutrality ended in 1948 when it joined the Benelux Customs Union and then NATO the following year.

This country has a GDP per capita of over $128,000 — one of the highest in the world — fueled by a financial services and banking sector that punches far above the nation's tiny physical size of just 2,586 sq km.

This country exports iron blocks and gas turbines as its top commodities, a legacy of an iron and steel industry that once exploited iron ore deposits now entirely exhausted, leaving banking and finance to dominate its modern economy.

name: Latvia
funFacts: This country's name originates from the Latgalians, one of four eastern Baltic tribes who formed the ethnic core of the Latvian people between the 8th and 12th centuries — making its national identity rooted in a tribal confederation that predates most European nation-states.

This country has amber listed among its natural resources alongside peat, limestone, and timber — Baltic amber, fossilized tree resin from ancient forests, has been harvested and traded from this coastline for thousands of years.

This country exports wood as its single largest commodity, reflecting extensive forests that cover over half its land area, followed by wheat, broadcasting equipment, and packaged medicine — a mix of raw materials and light manufacturing.

This country has a Russian-speaking minority comprising nearly 34% of its population — the largest proportional Russian minority in any EU or NATO member state — a legacy of Soviet-era migration that continues to shape its domestic politics.

This country has the white wagtail as its national bird, and its capital Riga is home to one of Europe's largest collections of Art Nouveau architecture, with over 800 buildings in that style concentrated in a single city district.

name: Morocco
funFacts: This country's English name derives from the city of Marrakesh — Portuguese and Spanish explorers called the country 'Marruecos' and 'Marrocos,' both rooted in the Arabic name for Marrakesh — making the nation's name a European adaptation of a city name.

This country's national holiday, Throne Day, commemorates the accession of King Mohammed VI on 30 July 1999 — rather than independence — reflecting that the monarchy's continuity is treated as a more defining national identity than liberation from France.

This country exports fertilizers, cars, garments, insulated wire, and tomatoes as its top five commodities — a mix of heavy industrial goods, manufactured items, and fresh agricultural produce unlike any other African exporter.

This country's industries include aerospace manufacturing alongside phosphate mining and automotive parts production — one of the only African nations with a significant aviation-industry sector alongside traditional mineral extraction.

This country's top export is fertilizers — derived from its extensive phosphate deposits — making it the only African nation where phosphate-derived chemicals rank above petroleum, gold, and diamonds in export value.

name: Monaco
funFacts: This country is the most densely populated sovereign state in the world and is 100% urbanized, occupying just 2 sq km on the French Riviera with only France as its sole neighboring country.
This country's ruling House of Grimaldi first seized control of the territory in 1297 and has held power ever since — making it one of the longest-ruling dynasties in European history.

This country has a GDP per capita exceeding $270,000 — the highest in the world — sustained by banking, insurance, tourism, and its famous casino, which opened in the late 19th century after a railroad connection to France was built.
This country has no agricultural land and produces no agricultural products whatsoever, importing everything it consumes while exporting jewelry, perfumes, watches, and packaged medicines.

This country's name may derive from the Greek word monoikos meaning 'solitary,' the Ligurian word monegu meaning 'rock,' or the Basque word muno meaning 'mountain' — reflecting its ancient origins as a Greek colonial outpost in the 6th century B.C.

name: Moldova
funFacts: This country is the only European nation whose name comes from a river in a neighboring country — the Moldova River in eastern Romania — with the river name itself deriving from an Indo-European root meaning 'dark' or 'black.'

This country has Russian military forces stationed on its territory in the breakaway region of Transnistria, east of the Nistru River, a presence that has persisted since independence from the Soviet Union in 1991.

This country has the highest proportion of agricultural land of any European state on this list, with 74.1% of its territory used for farming, and its top agricultural exports include sunflower seeds, grapes, and seed oils.

This country's official language is listed as Moldovan/Romanian — a politically charged distinction — with nearly a quarter of its speakers identifying their language as Romanian and the rest as Moldovan, reflecting deep divisions over national identity.
This country is landlocked, bordered only by Romania to the west and Ukraine to the north, east, and south — and its GDP per capita of just $16,500 makes it one of the poorest countries in Europe.

name: Madagascar
funFacts: This country's name was mistakenly coined by 13th-century Venetian explorer Marco Polo, who confused the island with the Somali port of Mogadishu — one of the few nations whose name arose from a case of geographic confusion.

This country exports vanilla and cloves among its top export commodities alongside garments and nickel — one of the few nations where aromatic spices and heavy industrial metals appear together in the same top-five export list.
This country's natural resources include graphite, chromite, rare earth elements, and semiprecious stones — one of the most diverse mineral and gemstone profiles of any African island nation.

This country's national symbols are the traveller's palm (ravenala) — a distinctive fan-shaped tree — and the zebu, a humped cattle breed that reflects the island's Southeast Asian cultural heritage among its earliest settlers.
This country's 4,828-kilometer coastline is one of the longest of any island nation in the Indian Ocean, reflecting the size of the island and the deep embayments of its eastern and western shores.

name: Maldives
funFacts: This country's highest point is identified in the factbook as the 8th tee of a golf course on Villingi Island at only 5 meters above sea level — the only nation in the world whose factbook lists a golf course feature as its highest geographic point.

This country's natural resources are listed as only fish — the sparsest resource profile of any sovereign nation in South Asia — yet achieves a GDP per capita of $23,400, the highest in South Asia, through tourism and fish processing.

This country exports aircraft among its top five commodities alongside fish and refined petroleum — commercial aviation assets appearing in a top-five export list for a tiny archipelago nation, reflecting the transit and leasing of aircraft through its maritime hub economy.

This country's area of only 298 square kilometers makes it the smallest nation in South Asia — a low-lying coral atoll archipelago with no land neighbors, its entire territory barely above sea level at a maximum elevation of 5 meters.

This country has no land borders and lists fish as its only natural resource, yet its national symbols include both the coconut palm and the yellowfin tuna — a pairing of a terrestrial tree and a pelagic ocean fish that together define the dual land-and-sea nature of atoll life.

name: Mexico
funFacts: This country's highest point is a volcano — Volcan Pico de Orizaba at 5,636 m — and its name may derive from a Nahuatl word meaning 'the center of the moon.'
This country's top exports are cars, vehicle parts and accessories, crude petroleum, trucks, and computers, with 76% of all exports going to a single northern trading partner.
This country was the site of multiple advanced Amerindian civilizations — including the Olmec, Toltec, Teotihuacan, Zapotec, Maya, and Aztec — before Spanish conquest in the early 16th century.
This country's population is 62% Mestizo (Indigenous-Spanish mix) and 21% predominantly Indigenous, and its official name is the United Mexican States.
This country lists silver and antimony among its top natural resources, and more than half of its total land area — 50.7% — is classified as agricultural land.

name: Marshall Islands
funFacts: This country's highest point is only 14 meters above sea level on Maloelap Atoll — one of the lowest national high points in the world — an atoll archipelago whose entire territory is barely above sea level and acutely vulnerable to sea level rise.

This country exports ships as its top commodity — maritime vessel registration and re-export being its primary trade activity — the only Pacific Island nation whose number-one export is ships, a reflection of its open registry program rather than any domestic shipbuilding industry.

This country's export partners are spread across the United Kingdom, Germany, Denmark, Ghana, and Cyprus — a geographically scattered list with no Pacific neighbors among its top buyers — reflecting that ship registration statistics drive trade data rather than the export of locally produced goods.

This country's natural resources include deep seabed minerals alongside coconut products and marine products — one of the few Pacific nations to formally list deep-ocean mineral deposits as a named resource, reflecting potential nodule fields within its exclusive economic zone.

This country gained independence on 21 October 1986 from a US-administered UN trusteeship — one of the last Pacific Island nations to achieve sovereignty — its political status having been tied to the post-World War II strategic interests of the United States in the central Pacific.

name: North Macedonia
funFacts: This country changed its official name from 'Republic of Macedonia' to 'Republic of North Macedonia' in 2019 under the Prespa Agreement with Greece, which had objected for decades that the previous name implied territorial claims over the Greek province of Macedonia.

This country exports reaction and catalytic products as its single largest export commodity to Germany, which receives 39% of all its exports — a concentration on a single partner that is among the highest in Europe.

This country is landlocked, bordered by five countries — Albania, Bulgaria, Greece, Kosovo, and Serbia — and its Vardar River valley serves as the main geographic artery through the otherwise mountainous terrain.

This country has two official languages: Macedonian and Albanian — the latter elevated to national official status in 2018 following an armed ethnic Albanian insurgency in 2001 and a peace agreement known as the Ohrid Framework.

This country's national symbol is an eight-rayed sun, echoing the ancient Vergina Sun — a symbol at the center of its long-running dispute with Greece over Macedonian identity and historical heritage.

name: Mali
funFacts: This country's national symbol is the Great Mosque of Djenne — one of the only nations in the world to choose a specific architectural landmark rather than an animal, plant, or celestial symbol as its primary national emblem.
This country sends 73% of its exports to the UAE — primarily gold — one of the most UAE-dependent African economies, with nearly three-quarters of all exports flowing to a single Gulf state.

This country is named after the Mali Empire that ruled the region between the 13th and 16th centuries — a medieval West African state whose historical reach across the Sahel gave both the country and a wider geographic identity their names.

This country exports gum resins — a natural tree sap with ancient uses in medicine, food, and incense — among its top five commodities alongside gold and cotton, one of the few African nations where this ancient trade product still appears in official export data.

This country's highest point, Hombori Tondo at 1,155 meters, is one of the lower national high points among landlocked West African nations — reflecting that most of its vast 1,240,192 square kilometers consist of flat Saharan and Sahelian terrain.

name: Malta
funFacts: This country is a small island nation in the center of the Mediterranean with no land borders whatsoever, yet its civilization dates back thousands of years and it boasts some of the oldest megalithic sites in the world.

This country exports refined petroleum, integrated circuits, packaged medicines, and even postage stamps and documents as top commodities — a uniquely eclectic export profile reflecting its role as a transshipment and financial hub.

This country's largest export partner is Nigeria (28%), which far outpaces its next trading partner Germany (10%) — an unusual trade relationship driven heavily by ship and petroleum trade through its strategic Mediterranean position.

This country's ethnic makeup traces back to ancient Carthaginians and Phoenicians, with strong Italian and other Mediterranean elements — making it linguistically and culturally distinct from any of its larger neighbors.

This country was under British rule from 1814 until independence in 1964, and its staunch support for the UK in both World Wars led to the island being awarded the George Cross — which still appears on its national flag.

name: Burma
funFacts: This country exports rare-earth metal compounds as a top-five commodity alongside garments and natural gas — the only Southeast Asian nation whose top-five export list includes rare-earth materials, reflecting deposits of minerals critical to electronics and clean-energy manufacturing.

This country's national symbol is the chinthe — a mythical lion that traditionally guards Buddhist temple entrances — making it one of the few Southeast Asian nations whose primary national emblem is a creature drawn directly from Buddhist religious iconography.

This country's industries explicitly list jade and gems as a named sector alongside timber, copper, and textiles — reflecting its position as one of the world's primary sources of rubies, sapphires, and jade, materials that appear in both its industries and natural resources.

This country exports dried legumes as a top-five commodity — a dried pulse crop unusual in a top-five list alongside natural gas and rare-earth metal compounds — reflecting its significant agricultural output of beans and lentils alongside mineral extraction.

This country's natural resources include marble and limestone alongside antimony, zinc, tungsten, copper, precious stones, and hydropower — an industrial mineral profile spanning construction materials, metalworking, gemstone production, and energy that appears in no other Southeast Asian nation's resource list.

name: Montenegro
funFacts: This country's name translates to 'Black Mountain' in both Italian (Montenegro) and Serbian (Crna Gora), referring to the dark coniferous forests covering its mountainous terrain.
This country declared independence from the State Union of Serbia and Montenegro as recently as 3 June 2006, making it one of the youngest sovereign states in Europe.

This country exports electricity and aluminum as its top two commodities, powered by its hydroelectric potential — its most significant natural resource alongside bauxite deposits used in aluminum production.
This country sends 38% of its exports to Italy, its single largest trading partner, a figure far exceeding any other partner and reflecting the deep economic ties across the Adriatic Sea.

This country was a semi-autonomous theocracy ruled by bishop princes under Ottoman suzerainty from 1496 until 1852, when it transitioned to a secular principality, and eventually gained internationally recognized independence at the Congress of Berlin in 1878.

name: Mongolia
funFacts: This country sends 92% of its exports to China — the highest export concentration to a single partner of any Asian nation — reflecting that virtually all of its mined coal, copper ore, gold, and iron ore flows through a single trading relationship.

This country's lowest point, Hoh Nuur at 560 meters, sits entirely above sea level — making it the only Asian nation whose entire territory lies above sea level — a landlocked plateau country with no coastal lowlands and no below-sea-level depressions.

This country's national symbol is the Soyombo character — a complex geometric symbol drawn from the Soyombo writing system invented in the 17th century — one of the only nations in the world whose primary national symbol is a character from an indigenous writing script.

This country borders only China and Russia — the world's third-largest and the world's largest country by area — its territory of 1,564,116 square kilometers wedged between two vastly larger nations whose combined area dwarfs most of the rest of the world.

This country exports coal, copper ore, gold, iron ore, and crude petroleum — a top-five list exclusively of raw extracted commodities with no manufactured goods, agricultural products, or refined materials — one of the most extraction-concentrated export profiles in Asia.

name: Mozambique
funFacts: This country's national symbols are a rifle, a hoe, and a book — representing defense, agriculture, and education — making it one of the few nations in the world whose official national symbols include an explicit image of a modern weapon.

This country's name derives from an offshore island named after Mussa bin Bique, an Arab trader who operated in the region — one of the few countries whose name traces, indirectly, to a historical individual from the Arab slave trade era.

This country gained independence from Portugal on 25 June 1975 — one of five African nations where Portuguese became the official language of independence — creating a Lusophone bloc on the continent distinct from Francophone and Anglophone Africa.

This country exports coal, natural gas, and aluminum as its top three commodities — an unusual combination for southern Africa, where most neighbors focus on gold, diamonds, or copper rather than coal and bulk metals.

This country's industries list asbestos processing alongside petroleum products, chemicals, and textiles — one of the few African nations where a mineral now heavily restricted in most of the world still appears as an active industrial sector.

name: Mauritania
funFacts: This country is named after the ancient kingdom of Mauretania (3rd century B.C. to 1st century A.D.) and the Mauri (Moors) people of northwest Africa — giving its modern name roots stretching back over 2,000 years.

This country exports processed crustaceans among its top five commodities alongside gold, iron ore, and fish — reflecting a significant industrial fishing and seafood processing industry on its Atlantic coast.

This country's export partners include Canada (12%) — an unusual major market for a West African nation — reflecting Canadian investment in its iron ore and mining sectors alongside the more expected Switzerland and China.

This country's natural resources include diamonds and gold alongside iron ore, copper, and phosphate — a mineral profile that spans precious stones, precious metals, and industrial ores rarely combined in a single West African nation.

This country's lowest point, Sebkhet Te-n-Dghamcha at -5 meters, is a coastal salt flat dipping below sea level — a rare feature in a country whose vast territory is otherwise mostly desert plateau standing well above the sea.

name: Mauritius
funFacts: This country's national symbol is the dodo bird — an extinct flightless bird that once lived only on this island — making it one of the only nations in the world whose primary national symbol is an animal that no longer exists.

This country was completely uninhabited until 1638, when Dutch settlers arrived — making it one of the few modern nations with no indigenous pre-colonial population, its people entirely descended from colonial-era settlers and workers.

This country's name honors Prince Maurice van Nassau, a 17th-century Dutch governor who never visited the island — one of the few countries named after a historical figure who had no direct personal connection to the territory.

This country exports diamonds as one of its top five commodities despite listing only 'arable land and fish' as natural resources — reflecting a diamond-cutting and re-export industry built on imported rough stones rather than domestic mining.

This country sends 10% of its exports to Zimbabwe and 7% to Zambia — two landlocked southern African countries — reflecting its role as an Indian Ocean trading hub that connects African inland economies to global markets.

name: Malawi
funFacts: This country's name derives from the Maravi people — whose name means 'flames' — one of the few African nations whose name carries an elemental, fire-related meaning.

This country's top export is tobacco — accounting for the largest share of export revenue — making it one of Africa's most tobacco-dependent economies, where a single leaf crop dominates in a way few other nations rely on.
This country exports tea, dried legumes, and raw sugar alongside tobacco — an entirely agricultural export profile with no petroleum, gold, or industrial minerals in its top five commodities.

This country's lowest point, the junction of the Shire River at only 37 meters above sea level, sits very close to sea level despite being a landlocked nation deep in interior Africa — its drainage flowing south toward the Indian Ocean.

This country's industries are dominated by tobacco, tea, and sugar processing — an economy built almost entirely on agricultural raw materials, with no significant petroleum, mining, or heavy manufacturing sector.

name: Malaysia
funFacts: This country's factbook describes its industries separately for Peninsular Malaysia, Sabah, and Sarawak — one of the only nations in the factbook to formally subdivide industrial descriptions by sub-territory — reflecting the physical separation of its two main landmasses across the South China Sea.

This country exports palm oil alongside integrated circuits, petroleum, and natural gas — one of the few Southeast Asian nations whose top-five exports combine a tropical plantation agricultural commodity with semiconductor technology and fossil fuels in the same list.

This country borders only three nations — Brunei, Indonesia, and Thailand — yet its position between the South China Sea and the Strait of Malacca makes it a central node in some of the world's highest-volume maritime trade routes.

This country's national symbols are the tiger and the hibiscus flower — the Malayan tiger alongside a tropical flowering plant — a pairing that captures both the wildlife heritage of Borneo and Peninsular Malaysia and the tropical flora of its equatorial climate.

This country's natural resources list tin alongside petroleum, timber, copper, iron ore, natural gas, and bauxite — tin being a historically significant commodity that made this region one of the world's leading tin producers before petroleum became dominant.

name: Namibia
funFacts: This country's name comes from the Namib Desert, whose name in the Nama language means 'an area where there is nothing' — one of the most stark and literal national names in Africa, describing one of Earth's oldest and driest deserts.

This country exports radioactive chemicals as one of its top five commodities — reflecting uranium mining operations that make it one of Africa's primary uranium producers and a supplier of nuclear fuel to global energy markets.

This country's natural resources include lithium, cadmium, tungsten, uranium, and diamonds alongside gold and silver — one of the most strategically varied critical and precious mineral profiles of any southern African nation.

This country gained independence on 21 March 1990 — not from a European colonial power, but from South Africa, which had administered the territory under a League of Nations mandate that began during the First World War.

This country's national symbol is the oryx — a large desert antelope supremely adapted to extreme arid conditions — reflecting the Namib Desert environment that defines its western coast and much of its interior.

name: Niger
funFacts: This country exports uranium and thorium ore as well as radioactive chemicals among its top five commodities — reflecting one of Africa's largest uranium deposits, which supplies nuclear fuel to power plants across Europe.

This country borders seven nations — Algeria, Benin, Burkina Faso, Chad, Libya, Mali, and Nigeria — more than any other landlocked nation in West Africa, placing it at the crossroads of the Sahara and the Sahel.
This country's name and the name of neighboring Nigeria both derive from the Niger River — creating two separate nations named after the same river, differentiated only by a two-letter suffix.

This country exports radioactive chemicals alongside uranium ore — one of only a handful of African nations to appear in global nuclear fuel supply chains as a direct exporter of fissile materials to foreign energy programs.

This country's national symbol is the zebu — a humped cattle breed — while its neighbors' national symbols include lions, eagles, and elephants, distinguishing it within a region where large predators and raptors dominate as national emblems.

name: Nigeria
funFacts: This country's population of over 244 million makes it the most populous nation in Africa — with more people than any other African country and roughly equal to the combined population of all other West African nations.

This country's industries include columbite mining — a rare ore that is the primary source of the element niobium — making it one of the world's key suppliers of a mineral critical for high-strength steel alloys and advanced electronics.

This country exports cocoa beans among its top five commodities alongside crude petroleum and natural gas — one of the very few oil-producing nations in the world where a major tropical agricultural commodity also appears in the top-five export list.

This country's name derives from the Niger River, exactly as its landlocked northern neighbor Niger does — yet the two nations named after the same river have entirely different demographics, economies, colonial histories, and geographies.

This country is the only West African nation with both a major petroleum sector and significant cocoa bean exports — a combination that makes its economy more diversified than most regional neighbors focused on a single dominant commodity.

name: Nicaragua
funFacts: This country's name was coined by 16th-century explorer Gil González Dávila, who combined the name of a local chieftain, Nicarao, with the Spanish word 'agua' (water), referring to the two large lakes in its west.
This country contains Lake Nicaragua and Lake Managua, the two largest lakes in Central America, and its highest point is Mogoton at 2,085 m.
This country's top exports are garments, gold, insulated wire, coffee, and beef, and the USA receives 51% of its exports.
This country gained independence from Spain on 15 September 1821 and experienced a Sandinista-led revolution in 1979 that shaped its political landscape for decades afterward.

This country's capital is Managua, and it borders only Costa Rica to the south and Honduras to the north — the most southerly of the five nations that simultaneously declared independence from Spain in 1821.

name: Netherlands
funFacts: This country's name literally means 'the lowlands' in Dutch, and only about half of the country sits more than one meter above sea level — with its lowest point, the Zuidplaspolder, sitting 7 meters below sea level.

This country's highest point is not on its European mainland but on the Caribbean island of Saba — Mount Scenery at 862 m — which became an integral part of the Netherlands after the dissolution of the Netherlands Antilles.

This country was the first European nation to grant formal independence to itself as a republic — the Dutch United Provinces declared independence from Spain in 1581, making it one of the earliest modern republics.

This country exports vaccines as one of its top five commodities alongside refined petroleum and crude petroleum, reflecting a world-leading pharmaceutical and biotech sector unusual for a nation of its size.

This country remained neutral in World War I but was occupied by Germany in World War II — a sharp contrast that shapes its postwar identity as a founding member of NATO and the EEC, and one of the earliest adopters of the euro in 1999.

name: Norway
funFacts: This country has the longest coastline of any country in continental Europe at 25,148 km — a figure driven by its deeply indented fjords — and its very name derives from Old Norse words meaning 'northern way,' referring to this long western shore.

This country exports natural gas and crude petroleum as its top two commodities, with oil and gas discovered in its adjacent waters in the late 1960s transforming it into one of the wealthiest countries in the world.

This country has twice rejected EU membership in referenda — in 1972 and again in 1994 — making it the only major Western European economy that has voted against joining the European Union not once but twice.

This country maintained armed neutrality through both World Wars but was occupied by Nazi Germany for five years from 1940 to 1945, after which it abandoned neutrality and became a founding member of NATO in 1949.

This country's only land borders are with Finland, Sweden, and Russia — making Russia its sole non-Scandinavian neighbor — and it applied to join NATO in 2022 alongside Sweden, ending its decades of informal post-Cold War military non-alignment.

name: Nepal
funFacts: This country's highest point, Mount Everest at 8,849 meters, is identified as the highest peak in Asia and the highest point on Earth above sea level — a superlative that makes this landlocked Himalayan nation the location of the literal summit of the world.

This country's natural resources explicitly include 'scenic beauty' listed alongside quartz, water, hydropower, and timber — one of the very few nations in the world to formally designate a landscape's aesthetic quality as a named natural resource in its factbook entry.

This country's independence dates to 1768 when Prithvi Narayan Shah unified it as a kingdom — making it one of the only South Asian nations never directly colonized by a European power, its sovereignty uninterrupted through the entire colonial era.

This country exports knotted carpets as its single top export commodity — a handwoven textile product representing traditional craft industry — the only South Asian nation whose primary export by value is a hand-manufactured artisanal good rather than a bulk agricultural or mineral commodity.

This country sends 67% of its exports to India — more than two-thirds to a single neighbor — the highest export concentration to one partner among all landlocked nations in South Asia, reflecting the economic dominance of its one open border.

name: Nauru
funFacts: This country's area of 21 square kilometers makes it one of the smallest sovereign nations in the world — a single phosphate-rich island in the central Pacific that was once among the wealthiest per-capita nations on Earth before its phosphate reserves were nearly exhausted.

This country gained independence on 31 January 1968 from a trusteeship jointly administered by Australia, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom — one of the only nations in the world to have been administered simultaneously by three separate countries as a tri-national trusteeship.

This country's exports are listed as only fish and phosphates — one of the most minimal two-commodity export profiles in the Pacific — sending 78% of those exports to Thailand, reflecting a near-total dependence on a single buyer for its fishing output.

This country's national symbols include both the frigatebird and the calophyllum flower — a seabird paired with a flowering tree native to tropical Pacific coastlines — giving it two distinct natural symbols from the same island ecosystem.

This country's industries include offshore banking alongside phosphate mining and coconut products — one of the few Pacific micro-states to formally list offshore financial services as a named industrial sector alongside its traditional resource extraction activities.

name: New Zealand
funFacts: This country's highest point, Aoraki/Mount Cook at 3,724 meters, is documented in the factbook as having been 3,764 meters until 14 December 1991, when an avalanche removed approximately 10 meters — one of the very few national high points in the world whose entry records the exact date when the summit shrank.

This country exports milk, wood, beef, butter, and sheep and goat meat — the only country in the Pacific region whose entire top-five export list consists of pastoral and forestry products — reflecting an economy built on temperate grassland farming and timber with no petroleum, minerals, or electronics in its top exports.

This country's national symbols include three distinct items: the Southern Cross constellation, the kiwi bird, and the silver fern — one of the most comprehensive national symbol sets in the Pacific, combining a celestial grouping, an endemic flightless bird, and a native plant.

This country has no land borders — an island nation with zero border countries in the South Pacific — yet achieves a GDP per capita of $48,200 through a diversified economy of agriculture, tourism, and financial services despite its geographic isolation.

This country's natural resources include iron ore sand alongside natural gas, coal, timber, and gold — iron sands being a specific coastal deposit of titanomagnetite found in its black-sand beaches that represents a resource form found in few other nations' inventories.

name: Oman
funFacts: This country's formal independence date is 1650 — the expulsion of the Portuguese — making it one of the oldest continuously independent nations in the Middle East, with sovereignty predating the American Revolution by over a century.

This country's national symbol is the khanjar dagger mounted above two crossed swords — a traditional curved blade that appears on its national flag — one of the most distinctively weaponized national symbols in the world.
This country sends 43% of its exports to China alone — the highest proportion of any Gulf state to a single buyer — reflecting a deep trade dependence on Chinese demand for its crude petroleum.

This country exports semi-finished iron alongside crude petroleum, refined petroleum, and natural gas — one of the few Gulf states to include a partial-manufacture metal product rather than pure hydrocarbons in its top-five export list.

This country's 2,092-kilometer coastline faces the Arabian Sea and Gulf of Oman — one of the longest coastlines in the Arabian Peninsula — and its maritime tradition is so ancient it was documented by Pliny the Elder in the 1st century A.D.

name: Pakistan
funFacts: This country's highest point, K2 at 8,611 meters, is identified as the second-highest mountain in the world — a peak on its border with China that stands as the most technically demanding of the world's highest summits despite being lower than Nepal's Everest.

This country's natural resources explicitly describe its coal as 'poor quality' — one of the only nations in the world whose factbook entry characterizes a named resource by its low grade rather than simply listing its existence — alongside limited petroleum and natural gas reserves.

This country's national holiday, Pakistan Day on 23 March, is noted in the factbook as alternatively named Pakistan Resolution Day (1940) or Republic Day (1956) — a single date associated with three distinct historical events in one nation's factbook entry.

This country exports rice as a top-five commodity alongside garments, fabric, and cotton fabric — a food staple appearing in a list otherwise dominated by textile products, making it one of the few South Asian nations to rank a specific food crop alongside manufactured textiles in top-five exports.

This country's national symbols include the jasmine flower alongside the crescent moon and five-pointed star — one of the few South Asian nations to formally designate a specific flowering plant as a named national symbol alongside a geometric heraldic emblem.

name: Panama
funFacts: This country is home to the Panama Canal, which was built by the US Army Corps of Engineers between 1904 and 1914 and fully transferred to Panamanian sovereignty by the end of 1999.
This country's top export is copper ore, followed by ships, refined petroleum, bananas, and fish, with China receiving 25% of its exports.
This country declared independence from Colombia on 3 November 1903 with US backing, after previously having been part of Gran Colombia following independence from Spain in 1821.
This country's highest point is Volcan Baru at 3,475 m, and it has a coastline of 2,490 km — the longest of any Central American nation.
This country's name may derive from a Guarani word meaning 'place of many fish,' and its national symbol is the harpy eagle.

name: Peru
funFacts: This country's national symbol is the vicuña, described as a camelid related to the llama — a wild Andean animal prized for its exceptionally fine fiber that lives almost exclusively in high-altitude South American terrain.

This country is described as the seat of several prominent Andean civilizations, most notably the Incas, whose empire stretched across much of western South America before Spanish conquest in the 16th century.

This country's exports are led by copper ore and gold, with China receiving 34% of all exports — a mineral export profile that parallels neighboring Chile's, making the two nations South America's dominant copper exporters.

This country's highest peak, Nevado Huascarán at 6,746 meters, towers above a 2,414-km Pacific coastline — a dramatic geography where glaciated Andean summits descend to coastal desert within a few hundred kilometers.

This country's name may derive from the Guaraní word 'biru,' meaning 'river' — an etymology connecting a Pacific-coast Andean civilization to an indigenous word more commonly associated with inland South American river cultures.

name: Philippines
funFacts: This country has no land borders — an archipelago nation whose 36,289-kilometer coastline is among the longest in the world — with thousands of islands scattered across the western Pacific reflecting a territory defined entirely by ocean rather than land boundaries.

This country gained independence from the United States on 4 July 1946 — the same calendar date as American Independence Day — making it the only Asian nation whose independence anniversary falls on the national holiday of the country that formerly governed it.

This country's national symbol is the Philippine eagle — one of the largest eagles in the world by wingspan and among the most endangered — alongside the three-stars-and-sun emblem, combining an endangered raptor with a geometric national emblem.

This country exports insulated wire alongside integrated circuits, semiconductors, gold, and machine parts — a top-five list combining electrical conductors, advanced semiconductor components, and precious metals in a profile unique among the archipelago nations of Southeast Asia.

This country's natural resources include cobalt alongside nickel, copper, silver, gold, and timber — cobalt being a critical battery mineral increasingly important to electric vehicle manufacturing that appears in relatively few Southeast Asian nations' resource inventories.

name: Palau
funFacts: This country sends 41% of exports to India and 26% to Turkey — two countries accounting for over 65% of its trade and neither a Pacific neighbor — with ships as its primary export, reflecting a vessel registration economy whose trade statistics are driven by maritime registry rather than local production.

This country's national symbol is the bai — a traditional meeting house used for community gatherings and decision-making — one of the few Pacific nations whose primary national symbol is an architectural structure rather than an animal, plant, or celestial object.

This country's exports are listed as only ships and refined petroleum — the most minimal two-commodity export description among Micronesian nations — an economy whose top trade data reflects ship re-registration and fuel bunkering rather than domestically manufactured goods.

This country gained independence on 1 October 1994 from a US-administered UN trusteeship — the last Pacific Island nation to achieve sovereignty in the 20th century — its independence coming eight years after Micronesia and the Marshall Islands achieved theirs from the same trusteeship.

This country's natural resources list minerals with a parenthetical emphasis on gold alongside forests, marine products, and deep-seabed minerals — gold being specifically highlighted within a broader mineral category in a way found in very few other Pacific nations' resource entries.

name: Papua New Guinea
funFacts: This country's national symbol is the bird of paradise — a group of birds found almost exclusively in New Guinea and its surrounding islands, renowned for their elaborate plumage — making it the only Pacific Island nation whose primary national symbol is an animal endemic to its own territory.

This country's industries list spice products including turmeric, vanilla, ginger, cardamom, chili, pepper, citronella, and nutmeg as named outputs — one of the most detailed spice production inventories in any nation's factbook entry — a reflection of its tropical highland agriculture.
